NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING AND AGENDA
NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS
Tuesday, October 24, 2023
ONE OR MORE SUPERVISORS MAY ATTEND VIA VIDEO AND/OR TELEPHONICALLY 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors will hold a meeting open to the public on Tuesday, October 24, 2023, in the Supervisors’
Chamber in the Navajo County Governmental Complex, 100 East Code Talkers Drive, Holbrook, Arizona. The Board may vote to
meet in a closed executive session to discuss certain matters and for legal advice on any item as indicated on the following
agenda, pursuant to A.R.S. § 38-431.03(A) (3). 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors finds that it is in the best interest of the community to conduct this public meeting using
a hybrid method in order to serve the public interest. 
Join Zoom Meeting, click here: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/87692173340?pwd=WDU3WWhlZFcxd1JqN1BzYXI1dUdpZz09 
 
Call In Number: 1-253-215-8782 OR 1-346-248-7799 (You may use either teleconference number)
Meeting ID: 876 9217 3340
Passcode: 271616
Persons with disabilities who need accommodation to attend or participate in the meeting may contact the Clerk of the Board’s
office at (928) 524-4053; at least 48 hours prior to the meeting, so an accommodation can be arranged.
Items on the agenda may be considered out of order at the Chairman’s discretion. A copy of the agenda background material
provided to the Board, except items to be considered in executive session, is available for public inspection at Navajo County
website, www.navajocountyaz.gov
“NOTICE TO PARENTS AND LEGAL GUARDIANS: Parents and legal guardians have the right to consent before Navajo County makes a video
or voice recording of a minor child, pursuant to A.R.S. § 1-602(A)(9). The Navajo County Board of Supervisors regular meetings are recorded and
may be viewed on Navajo County’s website, and social media pages. If you permit your child to attend/participate in a televised Navajo County
Board of Supervisors meeting, a recording will be made, and your child’s picture may be posted on Navajo County’s social media pages. You may
exercise your right not to consent by not allowing your child to attend/participate in the meeting.”

to 3 minutes. At the close of the call to the public, Board members may not respond to any
comments but may respond to criticism, ask staff to review a matter or ask that a matter be
placed on a future agenda.

NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS’ MINUTES
Tuesday, October 10, 2023
Present: Alberto Peshlakai, Chairman; Jason Whiting, Vice-Chairman; Daryl
Seymore, Supervisor District IV; Dawnafe Whitesinger, Supervisor
District V 
Staff

. Call To Order: Invocation and Pledge of Allegiance was led by Supervisor
Daryl Seymore.
9:03 a.m. Supervisor Fern Benally present. 
CALL TO THE PUBLIC:
Renee Rowles, 400 Freedom Lane, Taylor, provided documents and talked about
the benefits to the county and voters when precincts are drawn in accordance with
ARS16-411, indicating that it ensures that voters have sufficient and convenient
voting locations.  She talked about the upcoming school elections, stating that
there was an issue with having sufficient voting sites for voters.  She further talked
about the distance that voters will have to go to vote at the voting locations, using
the Blue Ridge School District election as an example.  She addressed the
increase in voters over the past four to six years and stated that she has not heard
any discussion about how the upcoming elections might account for this by adding
additional polling locations in the areas of growth.  She talked about the meeting
that was held regarding drawing precinct maps and urged that the follow-up
meeting be scheduled as soon as possible.

BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:
 
a. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration of Renewal of franchise agreement
with the Arizona Water Company:
Jason Moore stated that franchise agreements are agreements with public
utility companies that allow them to construct, maintain and repair their
systems that are within right-of-way off the sides of county roads.  He
indicated that the term of the franchise would be for a term of twenty-five
years.  He stated that staff recommends approval.  He indicated that Lee
Hetrick, Local Division Manager for Arizona Water Company, was present
to answer any questions.

Chairman Peshlakai opened the Public Hearing.  There being no
comments, the Public Hearing was closed.  
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to approve the renewal of the
franchise agreement with the Arizona Water Company, motion seconded
by Vice-Chairman Whiting.  Vote unanimous approving the motion. 
 
COUNTY ATTORNEY:
 
a. Consideration and approval of a Proclamation declaring October 2023 as
Domestic Violence Awareness month : 
Roxanne Pergeson, Victim Services Director, read the proposed
proclamation.  She stated that the numbers in the proclamation highlight
the need for adoption of the resolution.  She indicated that Domestic
Violence makes up over thirty-three percent of their overall caseload and
that it has been consistent for at least the last five years.  She stated that
there is a question as to whether this is a criminal issue or social issue. 
She indicated that this is something that they have to continue to talk
about and raise awareness about.  She talked about the event they will be
hosting for Domestic Violence Awareness Event on October 1, 2023, at
the Navajo County Fairgrounds and provided the Board with flyer
regarding the event.
 
Vice-Chairman Whiting thanked Ms. Pergeson and the County
Attorney’s Office for bring awareness to this.  He inquired about details for
the event.
Ms. Perguson talked about what the event will entail and what the funds
will go to support.  She stated that they do the fundraiser because they no
longer receive grant funding for it so use the funds to help with services. 
Vice-Chairman Whiting made a motion to approve a Proclamation
declaring October 2023 as Domestic Violence Awareness month, motion
seconded by Supervisor Benally.  Vote unanimous approving the
motion. 
Supervisor Benally made a motion to enter into the Navajo County
Public Health Services District Board of Directors Session, motion
seconded by Vice-Chairman Whiting.  Vote unanimous approving the
motion.

REGULAR AGENDA:
 
1. Consideration of the 2023 State Homeland Security Grant (SHSGP)
award to Navajo County Emergency Management :
Catrina Jenkins stated that there are three separate awards under the
State Homeland Security grant program.  She indicated that one goes to
volunteers for equipment that helps support public safety responders, the
second is for training and exercise, which is a regional award between
Coconino, Navajo and Apache counties and the third is for cybersecurity
protection, which is also a regional project, to support training equipment
software. 
Supervisor Seymore made a motion to approve the 2023 State
Homeland Security Grant (SHSGP) award to Navajo County Emergency
Management, motion seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote
unanimous approving the motion. 
 
  
2. Consideration of the 2023 Emergency Management Performance Grant
(EMPG) award to Navajo County Emergency Management :
Catrina Jenkins stated that this grant allows their staff to provide
emergency management activities for support to first responders and the
communities.  She stated that it’s for outreach, training and exercise,
response to disasters, that it supplies the alert system, plans, and
software. 
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to approve the 2023
Emergency Management Performance Grant (EMPG) award to Navajo
County Emergency Management, motion seconded
by Vice-Chairman Whiting.  Vote unanimous approving the motion. 
Supervisor Whitesinger made a motion to return to regular session,
motion seconded by Vice-Chairman Whiting.  Vote unanimous approving
the motion.
 
  
ELECTIONS:
 
a. Consideration of adoption of Resolution Number 39-2023 approving Poll
Workers and designating Vote Centers for the Special Election: 
Rayleen Richards talked about the reason that there are only being two
voting locations in Blue Ridge and three locations in Snowflake, indicating
that a majority of the voters get their ballots by mail.  She reviewed the
statistics for voter turnout at polling places for elections in 2019 and 220. 
She stated that the majority of voters in Navajo County vote by mail and
that’s why they determined where and how many polling locations are
set.  She talked about the cost that would be incurred to add an additional
  
                                                                    4 of 7 
DRAFT

<!-- page 10 -->
polling location for equipment and poll workers.  She stated that all of the
polling locations would be overstaffed if there was a hundred percent
turnout.  She stated that staff requests approval of Resolution 39-2023. 
Supervisor Seymore inquired if she had the numbers for the Holbrook
area.
Ms. Richards indicated that she didn’t have those numbers because they
have locations on the reservation.  She indicated that they have made
sure that there are enough polling locations on the reservation.     
Supervisor Benally made a motion to adopt Resolution Number
39-2023 approving Poll Workers and designating Vote Centers for the
Special Election, motion seconded by Supervisor Whitesinger.  Vote
unanimous approving the motion.

COUNTY BUSINESS UPDATE: Report from County Manager, County Attorney
and Board members :
Brad Carlyon talked about Bread of Life Annual Banquet that was held, indicating
that he and Sheriff Clouse did a pumpkin carving competition, indicating that his
raised $750.00 and that Sheriff Clouse raised $800.00.   
Supervisor Seymore invited everyone to Scarecrow Lane in Show Low, indicating
that it’s a fun event for families.  He stated that he had the opportunity to
participate in the 50th Anniversary of the Heber-Overgaard Fire Department.  He
talked about the history of the fire department, indicating that they have done a
fantastic job moving it forward.  He reported on visiting a transitional housing
facility to see how they run it, indicating that what they are doing is phenomenal
and that we need to learn more about it.   He stated that he is looking forward to
the CSA summit this week.
Supervisor Whitesinger reported on attending a partnership meeting in the White
Mountain Tribal Community with Cincinnati Children’s Hospital representatives to
5 of 7 
DRAFT

<!-- page 11 -->
talk about cardiovascular health.  She indicated that one of the alignments was the
Navajo County assessment that was done in determining health needs within our
communities.  She stated that the underlining need is to have collective discussion
around it.  She stated that yesterday she was able to attend the reading of the
Indigenous Peoples Proclamation by Governor Hobbs, indicating that there are
twenty-two federally recognized tribes within our state that have had significant
contributions and impact on our communities.  She reported on being interviewed
by Rebecca Montoya, a Counselor at Blue Ridge Middle School, who received a
grant to be able to do counseling sessions regarding connecting with people in the
communities who have overcome a challenge, stating that her show is Not all
Wounds are Visible.  She indicated that this also aligns with the work Navajo
County has done to assess the needs of the communities and being able to
support our community members and feel supported when going through adverse
times.  She talked about the numbers that are available, such as, 988 for
individuals going through a mental health crisis or contemplating suicide or 911 for
a medical overdose.  She indicated that we, as community members, need to
participate in these conversations and help educate one another about the best
place to reach out in a time of need and support those who are in crisis. 
Supervisor Benally reported on attending the groundbreaking for the Winslow
Library and thanked those who attended.  She stated that she attended the
Veterans Memorial in Birdsprings.  She reported on attending an event at the
Navajo Nation and indicated that she had a discussion with some of the kids who
talked about the issues with fentanyl.  She addressed the meeting she attended in
Kayenta regarding issues they have had with improvements to the playground,
indicating that a major issue is with drug distributions at the playground/
recreational area.  She indicated that one of her projects now is to pass a
resolution through the chapters within the Kayenta and Black Mesa region to have
a rural bus route study done.  She indicated that a study has been done in Window
Rock and Tuba City but that the Kayenta area needs to have one done.  She
stated that NACOG has provided a resolution template and that they are looking
into what can be done to get federal and state funding for it.  She talked about
Indigenous Peoples Day, indicating that it was a joy to know that it was changed to
Indigenous Day and that it’s important to the Native people to be recognized.  She
thanked Evelena Claw for coming out to the District 1 area to assess the roads and
help with scheduling a meeting with NDOT.    
Vice-Chairman Whiting stated that he is looking forward to the CSA Summit and
being able to work on legislative priorities with fellow Board Members and other
County Supervisors from around the state.   He talked about the coming
holiday season, indicating that there are a lot of charities and organizations that do
thoughtful and good things and that hopefully we have a chance to support some of
those and ways to help out.  He talked about the Giving Machine, which is a
vending machine, that will be located in Snowflake, where you can purchase items
that will go to the charities, indicating that some of the organizations are local, to
help them continue the good work they are doing in our region.  He stated that he
has had the opportunity to meet with some of the organizations and that he is
amazed at the good they’re doing year-round and how they support our
communities.  He thanked Melissa Buckley and those that were able to attend the
Bread of Life Banquet, indicating that he appreciates their good work.
 
ADJOURN: 9:59 a.m. meeting adjourned.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. f.        
Meeting Date: 10/24/2023  
Title: Indian Wells Chapter house as a Vote Center for the Nov. 7, 2023 election
Submitted By: Rayleen Richards, Elections Director
Department: Elections
Motion before the Board:
Resolution Number 40-2023, designating the polling places/vote centers for the November 7,
2023, election 
Background:
Indian Wells Chapter House was inadvertently left off of the Attachment to the Resolution as a
vote center which was approved by the BOS on October 10. The Indian Wells Chapter house
was always in the plans as a Vote Center for the Nov. 7, 2023 election. 
Attachments
Resolution 
Form Review
Inbox Reviewed By Date
Jason Moore Jason Moore 10/12/2023 01:31 PM
Elections Director Rayleen Richards 10/12/2023 01:38 PM
Form Started By: Rayleen Richards Started On: 10/12/2023 08:52 AM
Final Approval Date: 10/12/2023

<!-- page 488 -->
RESOLUTION NO ______ - 23 
 
A RESOLUTION OF THE NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS, 
DESIGNATING POLLING PLACES/VOTE CENTERS, PURSUANT TO ARS § 16-411(B). 
 
 WHEREAS, ARS § 16-411(B) provides as follows with respect to designating polling places: 
 
         “Not less than twenty days before a general or primary election, and at least ten days before a special election, the 
board shall designate one polling place within each precinct where the election shall be held, except that: 1.On a specific 
finding of the board, included in the order or resolution designating polling places pursuant to this subsection, that no 
suitable polling place is available within a precinct, a polling place for such precinct may be designated within an adjacent 
precinct. 
         and 
 
WHEREAS, on a specific resolution of the board, the board may authorize the use of voting centers in place of or in addition 
to specifically designated polling place. A voting center shall allow any voter in the county to receive the appropriate ballot 
for that voter on Election Day and lawfully cast the ballot. The voting center may be established in coordination and 
consultation with the county recorder, at other county offices or at other location in the county deemed appropriate. 
 
     
  
 NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the Board of Supervisors as follows:  
 
 That polling locations/vote centers for USD’s voting precincts attached hereto and incorporated herein as “Exhibit A”, 
are hereby approved by the Navajo County Board of Supervisors. 
  
 
            
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PASSED, APPROVED AND ADOPTED at Holbrook, Arizona on Oct. 24, 2023 
 
  
 NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS

<!-- page 489 -->
By ________________________________________ 
 Alberto Peshlakai 
 Chairman of the Board

________________________________________

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. g.        
Meeting Date: 10/24/2023  
Title: MGT of American Consulting, LLC Agreement
Submitted By: Leah Thomas, Deputy Clerk of the Board of Supervisors
Department: Administrative Services
Motion before the Board:
Contracts signed by County Manager pursuant to Board of Supervisors Resolution: MGT of
America Consulting, LLC - Cost Allocation Plan Agreement
Background:
The contract is for MGT to perform the County’s cost allocation plan (CAP).  Previously, we
had HeinfeldMeech PC perform the allocation, however they informed us at the end of the last
CAP that they were no longer providing these services to clients.  The County’s requirements
under this Agreement are purchased from MGT under and in accordance with the terms and
conditions of MGT’s Auditing and Consulting Services Contract #C-73-24-007-X-00 with
Maricopa County.
Attachments
CAP Agreement 
Form Review
Inbox Reviewed By Date
Finance Director Jayson Vowell 10/17/2023 11:15 AM
Clerk of the Board Melissa Buckley 10/18/2023 12:50 PM
Form Started By: Leah Thomas Started On: 10/17/2023 09:24 AM
Final Approval Date: 10/18/2023

<!-- page 492 -->
COST ALLOCATION PLAN AGREEMENT 
This Cost Allocation Plan Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered on October 10, 2023 (“Effective Date”) 
between MGT of America Consulting, LLC, with offices at 4320 W. Kennedy Blvd, Suite 200, Tampa, 
FL 33609 (“MGT”) and Navajo County, Arizona, with offices located at 100 East Code Talkers Drive, 
Holbrook, AZ 86025 (“County” or “Client”) to set forth the parties’ agreement relating to MGT’s provision 
of the below-specified Cost Allocation Plan services to Client.   
COOPERATIVE PURCHASING. County’s requirements under this Agreement are purchased from 
MGT under and in accordance with the terms and conditions of MGT’s Auditing and Consulting Services 
Contract #C-73-24-007-X-00 with Maricopa County (“Maricopa Contract”), attached hereto as Exhibit B 
for reference. The hourly rates shown in the Maricopa Contract have been utilized to create the fixed fee 
for County’s requirements in this Agreement. In the event of a conflict between this Agreement and the 
Maricopa Contract, the terms and conditions in this Agreement will govern. 
SCOPE.  MGT shall perform Cost Allocation Plan services for Client for a period of three (3) years in 
accordance with the Letter Proposal dated October 3, 2023, attached hereto as Exhibit A (“Services”).   
TERM.  The term of this Agreement shall commence on the Effective Date and expire on August 31, 2026 
unless otherwise extended or terminated in accordance with the Maricopa Contract.  
RENEWAL. The Parties may renew the Services in this Annex for two (2) additional one-year periods 
upon written agreement, but only to the extent that the Maricopa Contract is similarly renewed.  
MGT STAFF MEMBERS.  Michelle Garrett shall serve as Project Manager and point of contact for MGT 
under this Agreement.  
WORK LOCATION: Remote unless otherwise agreed.  
COMPENSATION. MGT shall provide all Services at the fixed prices below, which include all direct and 
indirect costs including meetings, document production, etc.: 
 Year 1:   $14,500 
 Year 2:   $15,000 
 Year 3:   $15,750 
Total:   $45,250. 
INVOICING AND PAYMENT.  Notwithstanding anything in the Maricopa Contract to the contrary, 
MGT will invoice 25% of annual costs upon completion of the initial data collection, 60% upon issuance 
of draft reports, and 15% upon issuance of final reports. Invoices will be in a fixed price format, not T&M.  
Client shall pay correct invoices within 30 days of Client’s invoice receipt. No payment shall be withheld 
or delayed by Client when, or to the extent that such delay is the result of Client’s failure to promptly review 
and accept the Services or to perform any act necessary for MGT to proceed or continue with providing the 
services. No prompt payment discounts will be applied under this Agreement. 
INSURANCE. MGT shall provide Certificates of Insurance to County that comply with the requirements 
in the Maricopa Contract unless other, County-specific insurance requirements are included in this 
Agreement.

<!-- page 493 -->
VENUE. Venue for any actions or lawsuits arising under this Agreement will be in Navajo County, 
Arizona.  
NOTICES. All notices given pursuant to the terms of this Agreement shall be addressed as set forth below, 
or if incomplete, then to the address on page 1 of this Agreement.

invoices.  Each invoice shall detail the work performed during t he billing period.

completion of the Project as approved by County.

Board of Supervisors Regular 3. b.        
Meeting Date: 10/24/2023  
Title: FY 23 Veterans Treatment Court Discretionary Grant Award
Submitted By: Kenichi Maruyama, Strategic Initiatives Manager
Department: County Attorney
Presented By: Brad Carlyon & Ken Maruyama
Motion before the Board:
Consideration and acceptance of a grant award in the amount of ($950,000) from the U.S.
Department of Justice FY 23 Veterans Treatment Court Discretionary Grant Program for
Navajo County Veterans Treatment Court Enhancement Project and authorizing staff to sign
grant agreement documents.
Background:
The Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) provides funding for selected applicants to plan,
implement, and enhance veterans treatment court (VTC) services, including program
coordination, management of VTC participants, ensuring fidelity to the model, and recovery
support services.
Navajo County was successful in obtaining an enhancement grant ($950,000) for the capacity
increase, systemic improvement, and additional services of the VTC. The proposed project is
modeled on the Ten Essential Elements of Components of Veterans Treatment Courts. The
project objectives include: 
Increasing the capacity of the VTC by 100% (from 40 to 80 participants) during the
4-year grant period, 
1.
Making systemic improvements through a designated staff position, a one-stop-shop
office, data management, professional development, and community partnerships, and 
2.
Providing more treatments, support services, and collaboration for veterans through
partnerships with Community Bridges Inc. (CBI) and ChangePoint Integrated Health
(ChangePoint). 
3.
The project goal is to restore more veterans to being successful, contributing members of the
community.
Recommendation: 
Staff recommend approval and authorization.

Project Description:
Navajo County, Arizona, proposes the capacity increase, systemic improvement, and additional services of its
Veterans Treatment Court (VTC). The proposed project is modeled on the Ten Essential Elements of Components of
Veterans Treatment Courts. The project objectives include: 1) Increasing the capacity of the VTC by 100% (from 40 to
80 participants) during the 4-year grant period, 2) Making systemic improvements through a designated staff position, a
one-stop-shop office, data management, professional development, and community partnerships, and 3) Providing
more treatments, support services, and collaboration for veterans through partnerships with Community Bridges Inc.
(CBI) and ChangePoint Integrated Health (ChangePoint). The project goal is to restore more veterans to being
successful, contributing members of the community.

Award Letter
September 27, 2023  
Dear JAYSON VOWELL,
 
On behalf of Attorney General Merrick B. Garland, it is my pleasure to inform you the Office of Justice Programs
(OJP) has approved the application submitted by  COUNTY OF NAVAJO  for an award under the funding opportunity
entitled 2023 BJA FY 23 Veterans Treatment Court Discretionary Grant Program. The approved award amount is
$950,000.
Review the Award Instrument below carefully and familiarize yourself with all conditions and requirements before
accepting your award. The Award Instrument includes the Award Offer (Award Information, Project Information,
Financial Information, and Award Conditions) and Award Acceptance. For COPS Office and OVW funding the Award
Offer also includes any Other Award Documents. 
Please note that award requirements include not only the conditions and limitations set forth in the Award Offer, but
also compliance with assurances and certifications that relate to conduct during the period of performance for the
award. These requirements encompass financial, administrative, and programmatic matters, as well as other important
matters (e.g., specific restrictions on use of funds). Therefore, all key staff should receive the award conditions, the
assurances and certifications, and the application as approved by OJP, so that they understand the award
requirements. Information on all pertinent award requirements also must be provided to any subrecipient of the award.
 
Should you accept the award and then fail to comply with an award requirement, DOJ will pursue appropriate remedies
for non-compliance, which may include termination of the award and/or a requirement to repay award funds.
Prior to accepting the award, your Entity Administrator must assign a Financial Manager, Grant Award Administrator,
and Authorized Representative(s) in the Justice Grants System (JustGrants). The Entity Administrator will need to
ensure the assigned Authorized Representative(s) is current and has the legal authority to accept awards and bind the
entity to the award terms and conditions. To accept the award, the Authorized Representative(s) must accept all parts
of the Award Offer in the Justice Grants System (JustGrants), including by executing the required declaration and
certification, within 45 days from the award date.
To access your funds, you will need to enroll in the Automated Standard Application for Payments (ASAP) system, if
you haven’t already completed the enrollment process in ASAP. The Entity Administrator should have already received
an email from ASAP to initiate this process. 
Congratulations, and we look forward to working with you.
Amy Solomon
Assistant Attorney General  
Office for Civil Rights Notice for All Recipients
The Office for Civil Rights (OCR), Office of Justice Programs (OJP), U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has been
delegated the responsibility for ensuring that recipients of federal financial assistance from the OJP, the Office of
Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS), and the Office on Violence Against Women (OVW) are not engaged in
discrimination prohibited by law. Several federal civil rights laws, such as Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, require recipients of federal financial assistance to give assurances that
they will comply with those laws. Taken together, these civil rights laws prohibit recipients of federal financial
assistance from DOJ from discriminating in services and employment because of race, color, national origin, religion,
disability, sex, and, for grants authorized under the Violence Against Women Act, sexual orientation and gender
identity.  Recipients are also prohibited from discriminating in services because of age.  For a complete review of these
civil rights laws and nondiscrimination requirements, in connection with DOJ awards, see https://ojp.gov/funding/
Explore/LegalOverview/CivilRightsRequirements.htm.
Under the delegation of authority, the OCR investigates allegations of discrimination against recipients from individuals,
entities, or groups. In addition, the OCR conducts limited compliance reviews and audits based on regulatory criteria.

Employment eligibility verification for hiring under the award
1. The recipient (and any subrecipient at any tier) must--
A. Ensure that, as part of the hiring process for any position within the United States that is or will be funded (in whole
or in part) with award funds, the recipient (or any subrecipient) properly verifies the employment eligibility of the
individual who is being hired, consistent with the provisions of 8 U.S.C. 1324a(a)(1).
B. Notify all persons associated with the recipient (or any subrecipient) who are or will be involved in activities under
this award of both--
(1) this award requirement for verification of employment eligibility, and
(2) the associated provisions in 8 U.S.C. 1324a(a)(1) that, generally speaking, make it unlawful, in the United States, to
hire (or recruit for employment) certain aliens.
C. Provide training (to the extent necessary) to those persons required by this condition to be notified of the award
requirement for employment eligibility verification and of the associated provisions of 8 U.S.C. 1324a(a)(1).
D. As part of the recordkeeping for the award (including pursuant to the Part 200 Uniform Requirements), maintain
records of all employment eligibility verifications pertinent to compliance with this award condition in accordance with
Form I-9 record retention requirements, as well as records of all pertinent notifications and trainings.
2. Monitoring
The recipient's monitoring responsibilities include monitoring of subrecipient compliance with this condition.
3. Allowable costs
To the extent that such costs are not reimbursed under any other federal program, award funds may be obligated for
the reasonable, necessary, and allocable costs (if any) of actions designed to ensure compliance with this condition.
4. Rules of construction
A. Staff involved in the hiring process
For purposes of this condition, persons "who are or will be involved in activities under this award" specifically includes
(without limitation) any and all recipient (or any subrecipient) officials or other staff who are or will be involved in the
hiring process with respect to a position that is or will be funded (in whole or in part) with award funds.
B. Employment eligibility confirmation with E-Verify
For purposes of satisfying the requirement of this condition regarding verification of employment eligibility, the recipient
(or any subrecipient) may choose to participate in, and use, E-Verify (www.e-verify.gov), provided an appropriate
person authorized to act on behalf of the recipient (or subrecipient) uses E-Verify (and follows the proper E-Verify
procedures, including in the event of a "Tentative Nonconfirmation" or a "Final Nonconfirmation") to confirm
Page: 9 of 19

<!-- page 524 -->
employment eligibility for each hiring for a position in the United States that is or will be funded (in whole or in part) with
award funds.
C. "United States" specifically includes the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands of the United
States, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
D. Nothing in this condition shall be understood to authorize or require any recipient, any subrecipient at any tier, or
any person or other entity, to violate any federal law, including any applicable civil rights or nondiscrimination law.
E. Nothing in this condition, including in paragraph 4.B., shall be understood to relieve any recipient, any subrecipient
at any tier, or any person or other entity, of any obligation otherwise imposed by law, including 8 U.S.C. 1324a(a)(1).
Questions about E-Verify should be directed to DHS. For more information about E-Verify visit the E-Verify website
(https://www.e-verify.gov/) or email E-Verify at E-Verify@dhs.gov. E-Verify employer agents can email E-Verify at E-
VerifyEmployerAgent@dhs.gov.
Questions about the meaning or scope of this condition should be directed to OJP, before award acceptance.

Restrictions and certifications regarding non-disclosure agreements and related matters
No recipient or subrecipient ("subgrantee") under this award, or entity that receives a procurement contract or
subcontract with any funds under this award, may require any employee or contractor to sign an internal confidentiality
agreement or statement that prohibits or otherwise restricts, or purports to prohibit or restrict, the reporting (in
accordance with law) of waste, fraud, or abuse to an investigative or law enforcement representative of a federal
department or agency authorized to receive such information.
The foregoing is not intended, and shall not be understood by the agency making this award, to contravene
requirements applicable to Standard Form 312 (which relates to classified information), Form 4414 (which relates to
sensitive compartmented information), or any other form issued by a federal department or agency governing the
nondisclosure of classified information.
1. In accepting this award, the recipient--
a. represents that it neither requires nor has required internal confidentiality agreements or statements from employees
or contractors that currently prohibit or otherwise currently restrict (or purport to prohibit or restrict) employees or
contractors from reporting waste, fraud, or abuse as described above; and
b. certifies that, if it learns or is notified that it is or has been requiring its employees or contractors to execute
agreements or statements that prohibit or otherwise restrict (or purport to prohibit or restrict), reporting of waste, fraud,
or abuse as described above, it will immediately stop any further obligations of award funds, will provide prompt written
notification to the federal agency making this award, and will resume (or permit resumption of) such obligations only if
expressly authorized to do so by that agency.
2. If the recipient does or is authorized under this award to make subawards ("subgrants"), procurement contracts, or
both--
a. it represents that--
(1) it has determined that no other entity that the recipient's application proposes may or will receive award funds
(whether through a subaward ("subgrant"), procurement contract, or subcontract under a procurement contract) either

prohibit or otherwise currently restrict (or purport to prohibit or restrict) employees or contractors from reporting waste,
fraud, or abuse as described above; and
(2) it has made appropriate inquiry, or otherwise has an adequate factual basis, to support this representation; and
b. it certifies that, if it learns or is notified that any subrecipient, contractor, or subcontractor entity that receives funds
under this award is or has been requiring its employees or contractors to execute agreements or statements that
prohibit or otherwise restrict (or purport to prohibit or restrict), reporting of waste, fraud, or abuse as described above, it

the federal agency making this award, and will resume (or permit resumption of) such obligations only if expressly
authorized to do so by that agency.

Reclassification of various statutory provisions to a new Title 34 of the United States Code
On September 1, 2017, various statutory provisions previously codified elsewhere in the U.S. Code were editorially
reclassified (that is, moved and renumbered) to a new Title 34, entitled "Crime Control and Law Enforcement." The
reclassification encompassed a number of statutory provisions pertinent to OJP awards (that is, OJP grants and
cooperative agreements), including many provisions previously codified in Title 42 of the U.S. Code.
Effective as of September 1, 2017, any reference in this award document to a statutory provision that has been
reclassified to the new Title 34 of the U.S. Code is to be read as a reference to that statutory provision as reclassified
to Title 34. This rule of construction specifically includes references set out in award conditions, references set out in
material incorporated by reference through award conditions, and references set out in other award requirements.

maintains, disseminates, discloses, or disposes of "Personally Identifiable Information (PII)" (2 CFR 200.1) within the
scope of an OJP grant-funded program or activity, or (2) uses or operates a "Federal information system" (OMB

Restrictions on "lobbying"
In general, as a matter of federal law, federal funds awarded by OJP may not be used by the recipient, or any
subrecipient ("subgrantee") at any tier, either directly or indirectly, to support or oppose the enactment, repeal,
modification, or adoption of any law, regulation, or policy, at any level of government. See 18 U.S.C. 1913. (There may
be exceptions if an applicable federal statute specifically authorizes certain activities that otherwise would be barred by
law.)
Another federal law generally prohibits federal funds awarded by OJP from being used by the recipient, or any
subrecipient at any tier, to pay any person to influence (or attempt to influence) a federal agency, a Member of
Congress, or Congress (or an official or employee of any of them) with respect to the awarding of a federal grant or
cooperative agreement, subgrant, contract, subcontract, or loan, or with respect to actions such as renewing,
extending, or modifying any such award. See 31 U.S.C. 1352. Certain exceptions to this law apply, including an
exception that applies to Indian tribes and tribal organizations.
Should any question arise as to whether a particular use of federal funds by a recipient (or subrecipient) would or might
fall within the scope of these prohibitions, the recipient is to contact OJP for guidance, and may not proceed without the
express prior written approval of OJP.

Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
Project Abstract 
 
Navajo County, Arizona, proposes the capacity increase, systemic improvement, and additional 
services of its Veterans Treatment Court (VTC). The proposed project is modeled on the Ten 
Essential Elements of Components of Veterans Treatment Courts. The project objectives include: 
1) Increasing the capacity of the VTC by 100% (from 40 to 80 participants) during the 4-year 
grant period, 2) Making systemic improvements through a designated staff position, a one-stop-
shop office, data management, professional development, and community partnerships, and 3) 
Providing more treatments, support services, and collaboration for veterans through partnerships 
with Community Bridges Inc. (CBI) and ChangePoint Integrated Health (ChangePoint). The 
project goal is to restore more veterans to being successful, contributing members of the 
community. The project addresses Priority #1A (promoting racial equity; removing barriers; p.9) 
and Priority #2 (implementing BJA’s strategies ; p.9).  
 
The Navajo County Veterans Treatment Court is held in the County’s Superior Court at 100 East 
Code Talkers Drive, Holbrook, Arizona, 86025. It is post-adjudication. With this grant, the 
project will enhance the VTC programs and system. The County requests $950,000 under 
Category 2 (Enhancement) for a 48-month project. The total number of participants proposed to 
receive services with this grant is 260 (50 in Year 1, 60 in Year 2, 70 in Year 3, and 80 in Year 
4). The minimum, maximum, and average length of program participation  are 3 months, 18 
months, and 9-12 months respectively.  
 
Based on in-house data, the project identifies veteran clients who are charged for misdemeanors 
as target population. This enhancement grant will help the County gain access to all evidence-
based withdrawal and treatment services. By partnering with CBI and ChangePoint, the project 
will provide treatment and services to reduce opioid, stimulant, and other substance use or 
misuse (p.14-15). The project will use BJA’s performance measures questionnaire to collect 
access and retention data (p.18-19). As an advisory board, the VTC Council will examine the 
data to ensure disparities do not exist in the VTC program.  
 
The project addresses NADCP's 10 Key Components of VTCs, particularly:  
• Eligible participants are identified early and promptly placed in the VTC program.  
• VTC provide access to a continuum of alcohol, drug, mental health and other related 
treatment and rehabilitation services . 
• Monitoring and evaluation measure the achievement of program goals and gauge 
effectiveness .  
 
Navajo County currently manages a Comprehensive Opioid, Stimulant, and Substance Abuse 
Program (COSSAP) site-based grant (Award #: 15PBJA-22-GG-04456-COAP).

Introduction 
Navajo County, Arizona requests $950,000 under Category 2 (Enhancement) for the capacity 
increase, systemic improvement, and additional services of its Veterans Treatment Court (VTC). The 
proposed project is modeled on the Ten Essential Elements of Components of Veterans Treatment 
Courts, a U.S. Department of Justice-supported guide for the successful operation of veterans treatment 
courts. The project goal is to restore more veterans to being successful, contributing members of the 
community. The objectives include: 1) Increasing the capacity of the VTC by 100% (from 40 to 80 
participants)  during the 4-year grant period, 2) Making systemic improvements through a designated 
staff position, a one-stop-shop office, data management, professional development, and community 
partnerships, and 3) Providing more treatments, support services, and collaboration for veterans.  
A. Description of the Issue 
The United States is mired in a decades-long overdose epidemic. According to the Centers for 
Disease Control and Prevention, the “third wave” of the crisis began in 2013, when the spread of 
synthetic opioids, particular fentanyl, caused overdose deaths to soar.1 The results have been tragic. 
From 2013 to 2017, overdose deaths increased nationally from just over 40,000 to 70,237.2 Federal, 
state, and local authorities sounded the alarm, making historic investments in naloxone distribution, 
public outreach campaigns, prescription drug monitoring, and other strategies. After overdose deaths 
stabilized in 2018-2019, however, the COVID-19 pandemic undid that progress and pushed overdose 
deaths to new highs. In 2020, overdose deaths jumped precipitously to 91,799.
3 In 2021, the United 
States passed 100,000 deaths for the first time.4

2 NATIONAL INSTITUTE ON DRUG ABUSE, Overdose Death Rates (January 20, 2022), https://nida.nih.gov/drug-topics/trends-
statistics/overdose-death-rates.  
3 Id. 
4 National Public Radio, Overdose Deaths Continued to Rise in 2021, Reaching Historic Highs (May 11, 2022) (citing data 
released by the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics), https://www.npr.org/sections/health-
shots/2022/05/11/1098314220/overdose-deaths-continued-to-rise-in-2021-reaching-historic-highs.

Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
Navajo County, Arizona has been hit especially hard 
by the overdose crisis. Located in northeast Arizona, Navajo 
County is a large (9,960 square miles), rural, high desert 
region with a total population of 106,717.
5 The county 
borders Utah on the north and includes parts of three major 
Native American reservations: the Navajo Nation, Hopi 
Nation, and White Mountain Apache Indian Reservation. 
The county seat is in Holbrook, a small town (pop. 5,053) 
186 miles from Phoenix and 90 miles from Flagstaff. The median individual income in Navajo County 
is approximately $23,000, while the poverty rate is 29%, more than double that of the state’s more 
populated counties. Compounding existing challenges, Navajo County has experienced extremely high 
COVID-19 infection and death rates in the last two years.
6  
Given its rural setting, high poverty rate, and the devastating impact of COVID-19, it is perhaps 
not surprising that Navajo County has suffered heavily during the overdose crisis.7 In 2021, Navajo 
County experienced 51.2 drug overdoses per 100,000 residents, one of the highest rates in Arizona, and 
a rate higher than every state except West Virginia. Sadly, these numbers are continuing to grow as drug 
supplies laced with deadly fentanyl enter the community and kill unsuspecting users.  
At the direction of the Arizona Department of Health Services, Navajo County created an 
Overdose Fatality Review team in 2020. Its annual report for that year provides a wealth of data 
regarding the regional overdose epidemic. 76% of overdose deaths involved men. 64% involved 
white/non-Hispanic individuals (20% Hispanic, 12% Native American). 60% involved individuals aged

6 Navajo County has the highest COVID-19 infection rates in Arizona. As of May 7, 2022, the county’s infection rate was an 
astounding 34,030 cases per 100,000 people. Weekly COVID-198 Update, AZCENTRAL.COM (May 11, 2022), 
https://www.azcentral.com/story/news/local/arizona-health/2022/05/11/arizona-covid-19-weekly-update-adds-5-490-cases-
41-deaths/9730829002/. Nearly 1,000 county residents have died of the virus to date. 
7 Like all of Arizona, Navajo County has been under a state of emergency since June 5, 2017, when the Governor declared 
the overdose epidemic to be a public health emergency.

Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
35 or older (20% ages of 25-34). Opioids were the leading cause of overdose deaths—52% involved 
opioids (not including fentanyl). Other common causes included methamphetamine (32%) and alcohol 
(32%). Of particular note, 48% of all overdose deaths involved fentanyl, most commonly mixed with 
heroin or methamphetamine.  
Individuals at risk of overdose are particularly concentrated in the justice system, where an 
estimated 33% of arrestees and 65% of prisoners have a diagnosable substance use disorder. Therefore, 
it is incumbent upon the justice system to take action to reduce overdose risk and protect lives. Although 
limited data is currently available, Navajo County’s Courts, County Attorney’s Office (prosecutor), and 
Probation Department have observed marked increases in the incidence of opioid use among justice-
involved individuals, particularly involving fentanyl. As a result, overdoses—which were relatively rare 
five years ago—are now seen on a regular basis. The number of people who got screened in the County 
jail has increased during the last three years: 4,602 in 2020, 4,675 in 2021, and 4,844 in 2022. 
There is room for improvement in Navajo County’s VTC system. The County has struggled to 
serve veteran participants with inadequate data, policies and procedures, information, and services. VTC 
participation may have been limited by lack of incentives and poor program awareness. With grant 
funds, the project will address these issues affecting the VTC system and programs. During the six 
months (October 2022-March 2023), 35 veteran participants were served at VTC. While 9 veteran 
participants were successful in completing the VTC program, 14 veteran participants discontinued their 
participation. There are several factors impeding veteran participants from completing the program, 
including court/criminal involvement (11), death or serious illness (2), and voluntary withdrawal (1).  
The County’s current operation of VTC involves a series of steps, including referral, screening, 
and assessment processes. Screening is conducted by both the defense counsel and prosecutor. They will 
examine a case, and jointly refer appropriate cases into Veterans Court. To be eligible for VTC 
programs, participants must be former members of the armed forces. They must be currently residing in

<!-- page 538 -->
Page 4 out of 20 
 
Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
Navajo County and able to comply with the program requirements. Indigent Defense creates a file for 
each participant  and places a large white sticker that says, “Military Service? Yes/No”, on the front of 
the file. The sticker provides an immediate verification that the assigned attorney has asked the question 
to each participant. The County Attorney’s Office conducts an assessment on each case and identifies  
the participants’ criminogenic risks, substance use disorder, or mental health conditions. 
The Navajo County VTC Council, including the defense counsel, the prosecutor, the judge, and 
the probation, meets monthly to review veteran cases, explore the various counseling and behavioral 
programs available to the participant, and determine the most appropriate program for the participant. 
The participant must agree to participate in and be subject to the rules, regulations and sanctions of 
VTC. In order to participate in a VTC treatment program, the participant can not have any other criminal 
charges or holds that will interfere with treatment.  
Programs are individually developed to respond to the needs of veteran participant s. The length 
and phases of the program are determined by VTC Council, but the program is designed to last for one 
year. Judges pronounce sentence at VTC in the same manner as they do at a regular court. Yet, by 
participating in a VTC program, veteran participants will be served better by VTC members who 
possess military experience, language, and cultural competency. The participants feel more comfortable 
communicating with VTC members, staff, and peer supporters. Building trust between veteran 
participants and the VTC system will contribute to increasing the participants’ program completion and 
reducing recidivism in our community. Judicial supervision is conducted in a collaborative manner. 
Under the judge’s leadership, the VTC Council holds frequent review hearings, verifies the veteran’s 
compliance with the program, and recognizes the accomplishment of the veteran in taking responsibility 
for their actions. The VTC Council members has received some in-house training on the VTC model. 
The County uses a team-oriented case management approach. The Probation Office takes a lead 
in administrating, developing, and facilitating the completion of case plans and treatment programs in

accordance with the judge’s order. The office provides community supervision, recovery support 
services, family support and mentor services. Probation officers work as a team, communicate with 
veteran participants regularly, and manage veteran cases effectively with community partners, including 
behavioral health services providers (CBI, ChangePoint, etc.), Arizona Health Care Cost Containment 
System (AHCCCS), Veterans Affairs (VA) Office, and veterans support groups (American Legion, 
VFW, etc.). In order to prevent and respond to risk for overdose, CBI employs veterans to deliver case 
management services effectively and responsively to veteran participants. CBI also conducts 
randomized drug testing by consulting with the County’s Probation Office. Probation officers serve 
veteran and non-veteran participants together. No designated officer is available for veteran participants. 
Some probation officers have military experience while others do not. Non-compliance with the 
treatment program could result in facing sanctions, including incarceration, community service, and 
reprimand by the judge. In cases of continuous non-compliance, a participant may be removed from the 
VTC program. Currently, approximately 40 veteran participants per year are identified and served in the 
County’s Probation Office. During the last five years, the number of veteran participants has increased 
by 100%, from 20 to 40. Restoring veterans to successful, contributing members of the community is the 
County’s VTC goal. In order to achieve the goal, VTC Council strives to examine each case thoroughly, 
analyze it carefully, develop the best course of action, and prioritize court resources and services for 
veterans with high criminogenic risk and treatment needs, including persons with repeat criminal justice 
involvement and SUDs. No fees are charged to VTC program participants . 
Navajo County is institutionally committed to enhancing VTC as part of its criminal justice 
system. The County’s Criminal Justice Collaborating Council (CJCC) was formed in 2015 with a 
collaborative leadership among the Sheriff, County Attorney, Presiding Judge, Chief Probation Officer, 
and Assistant County Manager. CJCC meets monthly to specifically discuss planning and 
implementation of different project initiatives. CJCC Director facilitates the group discussion,

Navajo County has partnered with behavioral health services providers, including Community

This strategy permanently sets the path for long-term vibrancy in the community. CBI deploys a team of

B. Project Design and Implementation 
The proposed project will be designed with a U.S. Department of Justice-supported guide for the 
successful operation of a Veterans Treatment Court. “In 2008, The Buffalo Veterans Treatment Court 
adopted with slight modifications the essential tenements of the U.S. Department of Justice Publication 
entitled “Defining Drug Courts: The Key Components”, (Jan.1997). There are key differences between 
Drug Courts, Mental Health Courts, and Veterans Treatment Courts. These Key Components
 provide 
the foundation for the successful operation of a Veterans Treatment Court” (Justice for Vets, March 20, 
2017). During the last decade, Navajo County has strived to develop a Veterans Treatment Court (VTC) 
with its limited resources and serve veteran participants better in our rural community. The County is 
committed to administering the VTC with a limited capacity, serving veteran participants with a limited 
capacity, and restoring more veterans to being successful, contributing members of the community. With 
VTC grant funding, the project will empower the VTC Council to make systemic improvements by 
demonstrating how well the ten key components are integrated in the system to better serve veterans.  
 Based on 25 years of empirical study on addiction, pharmacology, behavioral health, and 
criminal justice, the National Association of Drug Court Professionals (NADCP) has developed 
ten best 
practices t o dramatically improve outcomes for individuals involved in the justice system due to 
substance use and mental health disorders. The proposed project will apply these practices to make 
systemic improvements, including Equity and Inclusion (#2), Multidisciplinary Team (#8), and, 
Monitoring and Evaluation (#10). Attachment II (Logic Model) illustrates  relationships among the 
project’s resources, activities, outputs, and goals/outcomes.  
The County Attorney’s Office conducts an assessment on each case and identifies the 
participants’ criminogenic risks, substance use disorder, or mental health conditions. Based on the

<!-- page 542 -->
Page 8 out of 20 
 
Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
assessment results, veteran participants will be advised to participate in VTC, rather than a regular court. 
Veterans Affairs Social Workers collaborate with the defense counsel, the prosecutor, the judge, and the 
probation for the early identification of eligible veterans for referral to VTC.  
The project will make systemic improvements by taking the following strategies: 1) creating a 
designated probation officer position for veteran participants, 2) developing a one-stop-shop where 
veteran participants can receive necessary information about VTC, 3) building more effective working 
relationships with behavioral health services providers (CBI, ChangePoint, etc) to deliver treatment 
services to veteran participants effectively and meet their needs responsively, 4) improving data 
management practices, and taking a data-driven approach of decision-making, 5) examining the current 
policies and practices of VTC, identifying gaps or areas for improvement, and using evidence-based, 
best practices to enhance VTC’s operation as well as the County’s criminal justice system.  
In order to sustain project success, Navajo County will coordinate with local, state, and other 
federal resources and secure necessary resources to continue serving veteran participants in our 
community to the level of success the grant helps us achieve. The County’s CJCC meets monthly to 
specifically discuss planning and implementation of different project initiatives for a continuing 
improvement effort. Along with VTC Council, the CJCC will evaluate data of the County’s criminal

Native American population has been identified as the project’s target population in a data-

11.5% Hispanic/Latino, and 1.0% Black/African American, 0.6% Asian (U.S. QuickFacts). The County

residents are in poverty, which doubles the national average (11.4%). Native American residents have 
much higher rates of poverty: 37.5% in Navajo Nation, 30.5% in Hopi Tribe, and 39.3% in Fort Apache 
Reservation. In terms of educational attainment, 16.1% of county residents (25 years or older) have a 
bachelor’s degree or higher, which is less than half of the national average (32.9%). Native American 
populations have much lower percentages of the educational attainment: 8.6% in Navajo Nation, 7.5% 
in Hopi Tribe, and 8.3% in Fort Apache Reservation.

The mission of Navajo County Veterans Treatment Court (VTC) is to restore veterans to being 
successful, contributing members of the community. With grant funds, the project will allow the County 
to achieve the following objectives: 1) Increasing the capacity of the County’s VTC by 100% (from 40 
to 80 participants) during the four-year grant period, 2) Making systemic improvements through a 
designated position, a one-stop-shop, data management, professional development, and community

participants. Successful implementation of the grant will enhance the County’s VTC programs and 
system with evidence-based practices (e.g. NADPC’s ten best practices) to help restore more veterans to 
their rightful place in society. In order to make systemic improvements, the project will reexamine the 
County’s currently used assessment tool and explore a way to enhance the tool with evidence-based, 
best practices. The project team will review resources developed by American University’s VTC 
Enhancement Initiative. The project team will also utilize NADPC’s ten best practices to enhance the 
County’s screening, assessment, and case planning tools.  
Screening is conducted by both the defense counsel and prosecutor. They will examine a case, 
and stipulate that the case is appropriate for Veterans Court. The County’s VTC Council, including the 
defense counsel, the prosecutor, the judge, and the probation, meets monthly to review veteran cases, 
explore the various counseling and behavioral programs available to the participant, and determine the 
most appropriate program for the participant. The project will improve the County’s data management

 The proposed project will enhance Navajo County’s Veterans Treatment Court (VTC) by 1) 
Increasing the capacity of the County’s VTC by 100% (from 40 to 80 participants) during the 4-year 
grant period, 2) Making systemic improvements through a designated staff position, a one-stop-shop

more treatments, support services, and collaboration for veteran participants. With grant funds, the 
project will implement, enhance, and sustain evidence-based treatment and recovery support programs 
and systems for veterans in the County’s criminal justice system who have substance use disorders. 
All participants will be drug tested a minimum of three times per week in phase one, three times 
per week in phase two, twice per week in phase three, and no less than bi-weekly in phase four. Drug 
tests may occur more frequently in any phase if the Veteran’s Court team, probation officer or 
surveillance officer determines that more frequently tests may be needed due to the individual needs of 
the Veteran’s Court participant. All Phase I participants will be seen a minimum of three times weekly.  
Currently, the VTC Council meets once a month to conduct judicial status hearings. In the 
project, the VTC Council will examine its policies and procedures for improvement. The project will 
help us ensure that procedures are consistent at those status hearings by following our newly drafted 
policy manual. Given that our program is currently a post-conviction program, most concerns about 
procedural due process will have been addressed before a participant is ever enrolled. However, within 
the program, Judge, Prosecutor, and Defense Attorney will cooperate to ensure the law is followed. 
Finally, participant s may address the court at every VTC meeting, and can self-report any concerns or 
problems at that time.

C. Capabilities and Competencies 
Motivated by the continued impact of the overdose crisis on individuals and families involved in 
the justice system, Navajo County is committed to scaling up its VTC program’s capacity, providing 
more treatment and other critical  support services for eligible veterans, enhancing VTC operations and 
services, and improving collection and use of key treatment court operation and outcome data. This 
grant allows the County to support a new multi-agency initiative to better serve veterans in need. Staff 
members from the Superior Court, County Attorney’s Office, Probation Department, and Sheriff’s 
Office (Jail) will be contributing their time and expertise to making this project successful. The County’s 
CJCC intends to sustain systemic improvements after the grant period as an ongoing feature of the 
County’s commitment to serving veteran residents.

D. Data Collection Plan & Performance Measures 
This grant requires successful applicants to report the two sets of performance data. First, the 
Office of Justice Program (OJP) requires successful applicants to submit performance data that show the 
completed work’s results. The performance data directly relate to the goals, objectives, and deliverables 
identified in the “Goals, Objectives, and Deliverables” section.  
Secondly, the Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) requires award recipients to submit 
performance measure data in the Performance Measurement Tool (PMT) and/or JustGrants. Based on 
BJA’s performance measures questionnaire, the project will collect data include, but not limited to, the

<!-- page 553 -->
Page 19 out of 20 
 
Navajo County - For Official Use Only  
following: # of incarcerated residents screened, # of cases assessed, # of veteran participants identified, 
# of veteran participants eligible for VTC programs, # of veteran participants enrolled in VTC programs, 
# of veteran participants declining the programs, # of veteran participants completing the programs, # of 
veteran participants discontinuing the programs, # of community partners & supporters, and % of 
recidivism. 
During the grant period, both care team and advisory board will review project data, identify 
operational challenges, and formulate adjustments to the program as needed. The core team consists of a 
designated surveillance officer, a criminal justice director, and a strategic initiatives manager. The VTC 
Council will serve as the project’s advisory board. The VTC Council consists of VTC Judge, County 
Attorney, County Sheriff, Jail Commander, Chief Probation Officer, and veterans community 
representatives.  
Dr. Ken Maruyama, Strategic Initiatives Manager, will assist in managing the project’s data 
collection, reporting, and performance measurement activities in coordination with VTC Council. Data 
will be reported monthly to the project team for review/discussion. Dr. Maruyama will assist the project 
team in analyzing the data and ensure compliance with OJP & BJA reporting requirements. Dr. 
Maruyama will be responsible for submitting quarterly, aggregated, participant-level performance and 
outcome data through OJP’s Justice Grants (JustGrants) and BJA’s Performance Measurement Tool 
(PMT) systems.  
Dr. Maruyama will assist the project team in development of a final project report that describes

impacts, and documents implementation challenges and lessons learned. The final report will assist 
Navajo County in sustaining the project’s improvements  beyond the grant period, inform OJP & BJA 
about the project’s successes and challenges, and offer guidance for other jurisdictions seeking to 
implement similar  projects.

E. Budget 
 
Table 1 summarizes the project’s budget. This grant will help Navajo County to create a designated full-
time Surveillance Officer position for veterans. The Surveillance Officer serves as the main point of 
contact to communicate and coordinate the County’s VTC programs. In total, $155,828 is budgeted for 
the full-time position, and $124,907 is budgeted for its statutory (45%; FICA, Medicare,  ASRS, etc.) 
and healthcare ($13,500 per year) benefit costs. The project budget includes three team members to 
attend two conferences and/or trainings each year. $2,000 per person is estimated at the costs of 
conference registration, airfare, lodging, ground transportation, parking and per diem. In total, 48,000 is 
budgeted for travel. $18,901 is budgeted for testing kits and other project supplies for veterans. 
$176,000 is budgeted for indigent defense services ($100/hr x 4,400hrs/year x 4 years) for eligible 
veterans. By consulting with the County’s behavioral health services providers (CBI and ChangePoint) 
about enhancement of treatments and wraparound services for veterans, $85,000 is budgeted per year. 
We think of the amount to be reasonable, allowable, and necessary to the project. In total, $340,000 is 
budgeted during the four-year grant period. Navajo County does not have a federally negotiated indirect 
cost rate, for which the County elects to “charge a de minimis rate of 10% of modified total direct costs” 
(OMB Guidance § 200.414). In total, $86,364 is budgeted for indirect costs. Navajo County requests 
$950,000 from FY23 VTC Enhancement Grant for the proposed project.

treatment and recovery (including 2x weekly

drug tests, and monthly court hearings) 
7. After clinical stabilization is achieved (usually 
around 90 days), move patients out of the program 
and resume prosecution of their legal cases 
8. Whenever possible and appropriate, offer former 
participants the opportunity to enter a drug court, 
mental health court, or other alternative to 
incarceration for longer term treatment

Board of Supervisors Regular 4. a. 1.        
Meeting Date: 10/24/2023  
Title: Overview of the WIC Baby Shower Special Event 
Submitted For: Janelle Linn, Health Director 
Submitted By: Ivy McCullough, WIC Division Manager
Department: NC Public Health Services District
Presented By: Kelsey Nies
Subject:
Presentation of the WIC Baby Shower special event that was held on September 29, 2023. 
Background: 
Navajo County is a rural area with limited breastfeeding support services and opportunities for
mother-to-mother interaction. Many of our WIC participants have limited access to
breastfeeding support services after leaving the hospital. There is a distinct need for
community-based lactation support for expecting and new mothers, a gap that WIC is working
to fill as a reliable breastfeeding information source.  The goal of the grant-funded special
project was to create peer relationships that would last past the event, support breastfeeding
initiation and duration, and help mothers set personal goals. This event allowed for continued
breastfeeding support and breastfeeding education in our community to those in attendance and
holding more events like this one would be a benefit to the community.

<!-- page 568 -->
The Importance of Education + Support
Source: azdhs.gov
Studies show that participant-centered breastfeeding education and 
support is the single most important indicator to breastfeeding 
initiation and duration up to 6 months.
Navajo County is a rural area with limited breastfeeding support services 
and opportunities for mother-to-mother interaction. 
There is a distinct need for community-based lactation support for 
expecting and new mothers, a gap that WIC can fill as a reliable 
breastfeeding information source.

new mothers and their support person(s) in their 
breastfeeding journeys.
2. To establish peer connections.
3. To gain new WIC clients.

Board of Supervisors Regular 4. a. 2.        
Meeting Date: 10/24/2023  
Title: WIC-CTR067944
Submitted For: Janelle Linn, Health Director 
Submitted By: Ivy McCullough, WIC Division Manager
Department: NC Public Health Services District
Presented By: Ivy McCullough
Motion before the Board:
Consideration of an Intergovernmental Agreement, Contract Number CTR067944, with the
Arizona Department of Health Services for WIC and BFPC services in Navajo County.
Background:
Navajo County WIC staff provide services to families in need. As a result, $1,268,234.67 worth
of WIC benefits were redeemed in 2022 at local WIC-approved grocery stores in Navajo
County. The WIC program in Navajo County has been funded since 1974 as part of the Navajo
County Public Health Services District. Currently, this program serves participants at five
existing clinic sites: Winslow, Holbrook, Snowflake, Heber, and Show Low. There is also one
outreach location in Pinetop. The Navajo County WIC Program provides nutrition education
and offers referrals as well as healthy foods for low-income families across Navajo County. The
WIC program supports women during and after pregnancy, assists in breastfeeding support, and
offers nutrition education and tips to caregivers of children from birth up to 5 years of age. WIC
currently offers telephonic, virtual, and in-person appointments in addition to self-paced online
nutrition education and virtual group classes hosted by the Arizona Department of Health
Services State WIC program. The WIC Program is a federally funded program.
Recommendation: 
To approve a new 5-year contract for WIC and BFPC services in Navajo County.

1. Background 
 
The Arizona Department of Health Services (ADHS) Bureau of Nutrition and Physical Activity (BNPA) administers 
funds provided by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for the operation of the Special 
Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) and Breastf eeding Peer Counseling 
Program (BFPC) for the State of Arizona. The USDA nutrition programs are discretionary, and each provides a 
specific service to women, infants, and children who are low income and at nutritional risk. The overall goal of all 
the USDA Nutrition Programs is to increase food security and reduce hunger by providing eligible participants 
access to nourishing food and supportive nutrition education. 
 
1.1. WIC Nutrition Services: 
 
1.1.1. The WIC Program accomplishes this goal by providing participant -centered services (PCS) 
including nutrition and breastfeeding information and support, specific supplemental healthy foods 
through the issuance of food benefits that can be used at ADHS -approved grocery stores, and 
referrals to other health and human services as an adjunct to good health care during critical times 
of growth and development. Service population eligibility for the WIC Program is based upon 
federal regulations such as participant category (pregnant and breastfeeding women, postpartum 
women, and infants or children under five (5) years of age), a household income at or below 185% 
of federal poverty guidelines, residence within the service area, and nutrition risks,  
 
1.1.2. To be considered as a WIC Local Agency, the organization must be a local public or private non-
profit organization, county health department, or tribal entity under contract with ADHS to provide 
WIC services according to the WIC Program federal regulations and state policies and procedures. 
The State awards a WIC Contract based on the ability of the organization to provide WIC services, 
potentially eligible population, need, response to the Scope of Work, information technology 
capacity, and available funds. The State determines and awards the WIC Contract amount based 
on a funding form ula using several factors such as a base level for a program to function, the 
amount of caseload negotiated with each Local Agency, and quality of performance, and 
 
1.1.3. Specific objectives for nutrition services (based on Healthy People 2030) are: 
 
1.1.3.1. To increase the incidence of women initiating breastfeeding; 
 
1.1.3.2. To increase the duration of women breastfeeding for the first six (6) months of their 
baby’s life; 
 
1.1.3.3. To increase the duration of women breastfeeding for the first one (1) year of their baby’s 
life; 
 
1.1.3.4. To increase the rate infants are exclusively breastfed at three (3) months and at six (6) 
months; 
 
1.1.3.5. To reduce the proportion of adults who are considered obese; 
 
1.1.3.6. To reduce the proportion of children ages two (2) to five (5) who are considered obese; 
 
1.1.3.7. To increase the consumption and variety of fruits and vegetables by those age two (2) 
and older; 
 
1.1.3.8. To increase the consumption of whole grains by those age two (2) and older; and 
 
1.1.3.9. To reduce household food insecurity and hunger.

<!-- page 597 -->
CONTRACT NUMBER INTERGOVERNMENTAL AGREEMENT 
SCOPE OF WORK CTR067944 
 
 
  Page 21 of 39 
 
1.2. BFPC: 
 
1.2.1. Breastfeeding peer counselors add a critical dimension to WIC’s efforts to help women initiate and 
continue breastfeeding. WIC breastfeeding peer counselors provide a valua ble service to their 
communities, addressing barriers to breastfeeding by offering breastfeeding education, support, 
and role modeling. They are familiar with the resources available to WIC participants and the 
questions a new breastfeeding mother may ask,  and recognize when to refer mothers to other 
resources when issues outside their scope of practice arise. In 2020 the USDA Food and Nutrition 
Service (FNS) released their new national breastfeeding campaign titled WIC Breastfeeding 
Support: Learn Together . Grow Together. As a part of this, FNS has developed training and 
technical assistance to equip WIC Programs with a framework for designing and maintaining peer 
counseling programs. Developing this training included formative research to understand barriers 
and motivators to implementing and sustaining peer counseling programs and develop training 
curricula. This Peer Counseling Training for WIC Managers, which is a training and technical 
assistance project that will be used as a model to aid WIC in designing, building, maintaining, and 
sustaining peer counseling programs that will improve breastfeeding initiation and duration rates. 
Arizona will be using this program to guide and develop the state peer counseling program, 
 
1.2.2. The discretionary peer counseling  services are considered an adjunct support to WIC 
breastfeeding services to help achieve the WIC Nutrition Services objectives regarding 
breastfeeding, and 
 
1.2.3. Peer counseling has been a significant factor in improving initiation and duration rates of 
breastfeeding among women in a variety of settings, including disadvantaged and WIC 
populations representing diverse cultural backgrounds and geographical locations. Peer 
counselors are especially effective in communities where role models for breastfeeding behaviors, 
knowledgeable health care providers, and cultural practices that include breastfeeding as the 
norm, are scarce. Combining peer counseling with the ongoing WIC breastfeeding promotion and 
support efforts has the potential to significantly impact brea stfeeding rates among WIC 
participants, and most significantly, increase the harder to achieve breastfeeding duration rates. 
WIC Local Agencies are strongly encouraged to provide peer counseling services in addition to 
the ongoing breastfeeding support to their WIC participants. Contractors must provide a 
breastfeeding friendly environment and have policies to accommodate participants and staff who 
are breastfeeding. 
 
2. Objective 
 
2.1 At a minimum, provide WIC services while allowing each Local Agency to prov ide, at their discretion, 
Breastfeeding Peer Counseling Services. 
 
2.2 In the event the Arizona WIC Program funding is depleted (e.g. government shutdown) the Contractor may 
request permission to continue operating their program utilizing local funds. The Contractor shall contact the 
Arizona WIC Director to discuss the feasibility of sustaining clinic operations and participant food redemption at 
authorized vendor locations. The Contractor may transfer funds to ADHS to ensure continued operation. 
 
2.3 Additional monies may be awarded under this contract for WIC Special Projects related to, but not limited to 
general infrastructure, breastfeeding promotion, nutrition services, information system enhancement efforts and 
client retention efforts.
