EXHIBIT A 
Description of Project Components

<!-- page 844 -->
Exhibit A-1 
EXHIBIT A. DESCRIPTION OF PROJECT COMPONENTS 
The following components of the West Camp Wind Farm and Gen-Tie are planned for construction 
in Navajo County: 
• Up to 104 turbines and associated 34.5-kV electrical collection lines  
• Up to two on-site substations and up to one on-site switching station 
• Battery energy storage system, 
• Between 6.5 miles and 25 miles of 345- or 500-kV Gen-Tie Line (refer to description of the 
Gen-Tie Line below for further detail)  
• Up to six permanent meteorological towers 
• Aircraft detection lighting system  
• On-site operations and maintenance (O&M) building and laydown yard 
• Access roads 
Wind Turbines and Collection Lines 
The Applicant is considering three models of turbines for the Project: the Siemens Gamesa 6.0-170, 
General Electric 5.3-158, and Vestas 162-5.6. All three models are standard production models 
commercially available from leading turbine manufacturers. All turbines used will be of tubular steel 
construction and be painted a non-reflective, unobtrusive color. Turbine specifications (Table A-1) and 
a generalized drawing (Figure A-1) are provided at the end of this exhibit. Final turbine models will be 
identified at the time of Building Permit application.  
Collector lines will be 34.5-kV conductors that carry power from the turbine transformer to the on-site 
substations. Wherever possible, collector lines will be installed adjacent to access roads. Collector lines 
will be placed underground except 1) where they cross sensitive resources (should that occur); 2) 
if unsuitable subsurface conditions prevent the use of underground trenching; 3) if project terrain is found 
to be unsuitable, as determined by the Applicant and confirmed by the County Engineer; or 4) if burying 
the lines would violate applicable laws or regulations. If underground installation is not possible, collector 
lines will be installed at grade and covered/compacted to meet applicable electrical and safety code 
requirements.  
On-Site Substations 
The Project is evaluating several Gen-Tie Line interconnection options (see option descriptions below). 
Under Gen-Tie Line Option A and Option C, up to two collection substations will be constructed within 
the Wind Farm Site. If the Project is constructed in two phases, only one substation under Gen-Tie Line 
Option A would be constructed per phase. Under Gen-Tie Line Option B, a single collection substation 
will be constructed within the Wind Farm Site. The collector substations will each step-up power from 
34.5 kV to the transmission voltage of 345 kV or 500 kV. Each collector substation is expected to cover 
approximately 5 acres in an approximately 30-acre siting footprint and will consist of a power 
transformer, a control house, and a substation superstructure within an approximately 8-foot-tall fence 
enclosure.

<!-- page 845 -->
Exhibit A-2 
Battery Energy Storage System 
The Project includes an up to 250-MW, 4-hour battery storage facility. The battery storage facility would 
occupy approximately 16 acres of land and be sited next to one of the Project’s substations centrally 
located within the Wind Farm Site away from adjacent non-participating Project landowners. The facility 
will be fully enclosed within an approximately 8-foot-tall fence. The battery modules will be racked (akin 
to server racks) within modular, external access-only containers that will connect to associated electrical 
equipment. The battery storage racks would be located within a metal frame outdoor-rated storage 
container with insulation and robust thermal management systems, with separate enclosures for the 
electronic controls and communications equipment, inverters, and transformers. The containers will be 
approximately 8 to 10 feet in height. Prior to construction and as a condition of the construction permit 
issuance, the Applicant will submit an Emergency Response Plan to Navajo County that outlines the 
technology capabilities and training program as it relates to fire detection and suppression. Furthermore, 
AES would conduct robust training with local first responders during construction and prior to operations 
of the battery storage facility. The facility would be monitored 24 hours per day, 7 days/week, 365 days 
per year in the Applicant’s remote operation center to ensure proper operations, in addition to continual 
on-site inspections and planned maintenance. 
Gen-Tie Line 
The Wind Farm will include a Gen-Tie Line interconnect to the existing APS transmission system at the 
Cholla Substation or via a line tap on the APS 345-kV Preacher Canyon-Cholla transmission line or APS 
345-kV Cholla-Pinnacle Peak transmission line within the Wind Farm Site. The conceptual Gen-Tie Line 
interconnection options are described below. 
• Gen-Tie Line Option A – Up to (2) two on-site substations located within the Wind Farm Site and 
an approximately 25-mile-long 345-kV or 500-kV transmission line to the existing Cholla 
Substation. Exterior to the Wind Farm Site, the Gen-Tie Line Corridor to the Cholla Substation 
largely parallels existing high-voltage transmission line infrastructure to the existing Cholla 
Substation.  
• Gen-Tie Line Option B – Single on-site substation located within the Wind Farm Site and an 
approximately 17-mile-long 345-kV or 500-kV transmission line to the existing Cholla 
Substation. Exterior to the Wind Farm Site, the proposed Gen-Tie Line Corridor to the Cholla 
Substation largely parallels existing high-voltage transmission line infrastructure to the existing 
Cholla Substation. 
• Gen-Tie Line Option C – Up to two (2) on-site substations within the Wind Farm Site, up to an 
approximately 11-mile-long 345-kV Gen-Tie to either the existing APS 345-kV Preacher 
Canyon-Cholla transmission line or the existing APS 345-kV Cholla-Pinnacle Peak transmission 
line, and single on-site switching station and line-tap within the Wind Farm Site. 
Exterior to the Wind Farm Site, Gen-Tie Line Option A and Gen-Tie Line Option B will be constructed 
within a 150-foot-wide easement. Within the Wind Farm, the Gen-Tie transmission lines will be 
constructed within a 500-foot-wide corridor. The location of the Gen-Tie Line corridor within the Wind 
Farm will be based on further electrical and engineering requirements. The Applicant is currently seeking 
approval of the Gen-Tie Line, Substations, and Switching Station from the Arizona Corporation 
Commission through Certificate of Environmental Compatibility proceedings. Final design and 
engineering details of all Project structures will be provided to Navajo County in future Building Permit 
applications.

<!-- page 846 -->
Exhibit A-3 
Under Option C, an on-site switching station and line-tap will be constructed within the Wind Farm Site 
for the interconnection with the APS 345-kV Preacher Canyon-Cholla transmission line or APS 345-kV 
Cholla-Pinnacle Peak transmission line. The switching station is expected to cover approximately 6 acres 
in an approximately 30-acre siting footprint. 
Under all Gen-Tie Line Options, the Gen-Tie line will consist of steel monopole structures with three 
conductor cables, plus two lightning protection and communication cables, suspended between structures. 
The tallest monopole structures are expected to be approximately 180 feet tall and will be spaced 
approximately 1,000 feet apart. At the lowest sag point between structures, conductor cables are expected 
to have a ground clearance of approximately 30 feet. Variations may be made to achieve site-specific 
engineering requirements. An estimated six poles will be required per mile of line, but additional or fewer 
poles may be required based on final engineering design. Pole structures will be sited to avoid recorded 
cultural resource sites. Line marking devices will be installed where birds may be at increased risk 
of collision per Avian Power Line Interaction Committee (APLIC) 2012 guidance.  
The Applicant is currently seeking approval of the Gen-Tie Line, Substations, and Switching Station from 
the Arizona Corporation Commission through Certificate of Environmental Compatibility proceedings. 
The final design of the Project’s Gen-Tie Line and associated high-voltage infrastructure will 
be determined based on electrical and engineering requirements and in consultation with APS. 
On-site Operations and Maintenance Building and Laydown 
Yard 
The on-site O&M building and contiguous laydown area for vehicles and equipment will be located 
on private land as shown in the Site Plan. The laydown area will include gravel parking and equipment 
staging areas, covered storage, “connex box” storage containers, and portable sanitary facilities. The total 
area required for the laydown area is not expected to exceed approximately 10 acres during construction. 
The O&M building and associated parking and equipment storage area will occupy approximately 10 
acres during operations and will be fenced for security and potentially monitored with surveillance 
cameras.  
The on-site O&M building will have either backfeed power or small generators to provide intermittent 
electricity. Nonpotable water is planned to be available on-site, with potable water to be delivered from 
off-site commercial sources. The on-site O&M building will only be used by occasional on-site workers 
for computer data entry, inspection report preparation, work breaks, and other similar activities. The 
O&M building will include restroom facilities with a potential septic system, subject to Navajo County 
approval of related construction permits. Potable water will likely be brought in from off-site commercial 
sources. Minimal nonpotable water use for O&M building restrooms will be supplied via water wells. 
An off-site O&M building may be leased or purchased in Holbrook, Arizona, or another nearby 
community. Operational parameters of the West Camp Wind Farm will be remotely monitored and 
controlled 24 hours per day from the Applicant’s control room in Salt Lake City, Utah. 
As with other project components discussed in this section, final designs will be provided in future 
Building Permit applications.  
Access Roads 
Based on preliminary geotechnical analysis, the subsurface conditions in the Wind Farm Site are expected 
to have sufficient bearing strength for normal road construction. If areas of weaker bearing strength are

<!-- page 847 -->
Exhibit A-4 
encountered, standard practice is to either compact the road or cement stabilize the road surface prior to 
applying aggregate and completing compaction. Final roadway construction, stabilization methods, and 
materials will be developed in the Wind Farm’s final civil design. Basic parameters for access roads 
include the following: 
• Where possible, construction crews will attempt to improve existing roads rather than install new 
roads. Most turbine access roads will be new or improved to achieve access requirements at each 
turbine location. 
• Roads will be built or improved to accommodate equipment in excess of 200,000 pounds and 
may require improvement or replacement of certain culverts and cattle guards. 
• Permanent access roads will approximately 16 feet wide with an improved crane path shoulder to 
allow crane access to all turbine locations.

West Camp Wind Farm Citizen Participation Report 
1 
1 INTRODUCTION 
This Citizen Participation Report includes information on the public involvement program conducted for 
the West Camp Wind Farm (Project) and the results from implementation of the West Camp Wind Farm 
Citizen Participation Plan (Appendix A). The purpose is to describe the methods used to provide 
interested persons, including project area neighbors, an opportunity to understand the proposed Project, 
located in Navajo County, Arizona, and provide comments on the project. 
A description of the Citizen Participation Plan implementation process and the results of the public 
comment process follows. 
2 NOTICE OF PUBLIC MEETING 
The public was informed about the proposed project and the associated public meetings using the 
following methods: 
1. Website—The Applicant, West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES 
Corporation (AES), developed a project website (https://www.aes.com/west-camp-wind) that 
contains project description information, including information presented at the public meetings, 
and a mechanism for public comment submittal. The website, which was announced in the legal 
notice and public mailings, provides an opportunity for persons unable to attend the public 
meetings to learn about the project and provide comments. 
2. Legal Notice—A legal notice was published on May 11, 2022, in The Tribune, a newspaper 
outlet which serves northern Arizona and the Navajo Nation (see Appendix B). The notice 
included a brief description of the project, the public meeting dates, times, and location, and the 
project website address for further information.  
3. Notice Mailing—Property owners in the vicinity of the project area and other potentially 
interested parties were notified about the public meeting by mail 20 days prior to the meeting 
(May 4, 2022). The notification letter included a brief description of the project, a project map, 
meeting dates, times, and location, and details on how to seek further information (website and 
mailing address) (see Appendix C). 
a. In Navajo County, 105 property owners within 1 mile of the project area boundary were 
notified. 
b. Interested federal, state, and county officials were notified, including Navajo County 
officials, the Arizona State Land Department, Arizona Game and Fish Department, 
Arizona State Historic Preservation Office, Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests, Bureau 
of Land Management, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. 
Other public noticing, including website updates, and additional mailings have occurred in connection 
with the Arizona Corporation Commission proceedings for the West Camp Generation-Tie Project. 
3 PUBLIC MEETING 
Two public meetings were held on May 24, 2022, in Holbrook, Arizona. The meetings were informal 
“open house” style formats, allowing community members to attend at their convenience, review 
displays, and speak with members of the project team. All attendees were recorded on an official sign-in 
sheet upon entering the meeting (three attendees signed in; see Appendix D).

<!-- page 897 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Citizen Participation Report 
2 
An overview of the Project was presented using the following handout and poster displays (see 
Appendix D): 
1. Handout summary sheet of the project 
2. Poster displays 
a. Overview of AES 
b. West Camp Wind Farm Project Overview 
c. West Camp Wind Farm Environmental Studies and Agency Coordination 
d. West Camp Wind Farm Overview Map 
e. West Camp Wind Farm Site Map  
f. Preliminary Visual Simulations (five poster boards) 
3. Comment forms were provided to solicit public comment on the project and the information 
presented at the meeting.  
4 TRIBAL OUTREACH 
Despite no federal permitting nexus and Section 106 National Historic Preservation Act tribal 
consultation requirements, the Applicant voluntarily contacted eight tribal groups (listed below) to inform 
them about the proposed project. The Hopi Tribe expressed interest in further involvement and learning 
more about the project.  
• Fort Mojave Indian Tribe 
• Hopi Tribe 
• Mescalero Apache Tribe 
• Navajo Nation 
• Pueblo of Zuni 
• Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community 
• Tonto Apache Tribe 
• White Mountain Apache Tribe 
5 STAKEHOLDER BRIEFINGS 
Project briefings with stakeholders included numerous meetings over the course of nearly a year with 
landowners; local, state, and federal agencies; and other local organizations. A summary listing of the key 
meetings conducted to date is included in Table 1 below. Note that ongoing and frequent coordination 
is occurring with various stakeholders and agencies, and is planned to continue throughout the 
development, construction, and operational phases of the project. The Applicant is also engaging 
in conversations with other local groups and non-profit organizations, and looks forward to becoming 
a supporting partner of several local organizations in the northern Arizona community.

6 PUBLIC COMMENTS 
At the time of the Special Use Permit application submittal in late June 2022, no public comments were 
received on the project. Following the notice of public meeting, AES was contacted by two members of 
the public. One inquiry was for additional maps and the other was for additional information on the 
location of turbines, turbine setbacks from residences, and public access on Hutch Road. AES provided 
additional maps and verbally responded to the Project inquiry. No additional follow up was received. 
AES also received a phone call from an Arizona Game and Fish Department staff inquiring about a 
“virtual open house” option for the public meetings. AES responded that there would not be a virtual open 
house and relayed further information about the in-person public open house. As described above in 
Section 4, the Hopi Tribe responded to the tribal outreach and expressed interest in further involvement 
and learning more about the project. Two agencies provided written (email) comments regarding the 
project. The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Safford Field Office provided a comment regarding 
access to the project east from State Route 377. The Arizona State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) 
provided a comment regarding cultural resource investigations and requested to review the reports when 
investigations have concluded. 
The comment letters and AES response are provided in Appendix E. AES will continue to coordinate 
with the BLM and Navajo County regarding access to the Project and with SHPO regarding cultural 
resources.

WEST CAMP WIND FARM 
CITIZEN PARTICIPATION PLAN 
Navajo County 
June 2022 
INTRODUCTION 
The purpose of this Citizen Participation Plan is to develop a collaborative approach for community 
outreach for the West Camp Wind Farm (Project) in support of a Navajo County Special Use Permit and 
Arizona Corporation Commission (ACC) Certificate of Environmental Compatibility. The West Camp 
Wind Farm, owned by West Camp Wind Farm, LLC (a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES 
Corporation [AES]), is located in Navajo County and proposes the construction of a 500-megawat (MW) 
wind energy facility and associated generation-tie transmission line located on private lands and Arizona 
State Trust lands.   
PLAN PURPOSE 
The primary purpose for citizen participation in the project is to ensure that citizens and property owners 
in Navajo County have adequate opportunity to learn about the project and resolve concerns, as much as 
possible, early in the process. This purpose will be met by: 
• providing the public with accurate and easily understandable information about the project; 
• providing opportunities for interested parties to get information and communicate their  
comments and concerns regarding the project; and  
• complying with Navajo County requirements for citizen participation. 
Citizen Participation Strategy 
The citizen participation strategy is designed to educate the public and interested parties about the 
proposed project and receive their input and opinions. The following mechanisms will allow the project 
owner to provide opportunities for public education and input:  
• Website—AES will develop a project website that contains project description information, 
including all information presented at the public meeting, and a mechanism for public comment 
submittal.   
• Notice Mailing—The public notice describing the project, public meeting(s), and comment 
solicitation will be mailed to all parties identified in the mailing list at least 14 days prior to any 
scheduled public meeting. 
• Legal Advertisement—An abbreviated notice that describes the proposed project and announces 
the meeting(s) will be presented 7 days prior to the public meeting in the legal sections of the 
following newspaper outlet: The Tribune (serving central Navajo County).  
• Public Meetings—The purpose of the public meetings is to share information about the proposed 
project with interested parties and to gather opinions and comments regarding the proposal. Two 
public open house meetings will be held on Tuesday, May 24, 2022. Both public meetings will be

<!-- page 903 -->
2 
held at the Holbrook Recreation Center, with the first meeting occurring from 12:00 p.m. – 2:00 
p.m., and the second meeting occurring from 5:00 p.m. – 7:00 p.m. AES and County 
representatives will attend each meeting and will be available to answer questions from the 
public. The meetings will be “open house” style with meeting materials consisting of five poster 
boards presenting the project (proposed project summary, location maps, AES company 
information, agency and environmental resource information), five visual simulation poster 
boards, a summary handout, comment forms, and sign-in sheets. 
Potentially Affected and Interested Parties 
The community outreach process will involve a wide range of potentially affected and interested parties, 
including government agencies and officials, tribal groups, media, adjacent landowners, and the general 
public. The following briefly describes each group. This is only a preliminary list and may be expanded at 
any time in the process if necessary. 
Agencies and Officials 
Public notices will be sent to the following agencies and officials: 
• Navajo County Commissioners 
• Arizona Game and Fish Department  
• Arizona State Historic Preservation Office 
• Arizona State Land Department 
• Apache-Sitgreaves National Forests  
• Bureau of Land Management (Safford Field Office) 
• U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Region 2 Migratory Birds, Albuquerque Office and Arizona 
Ecological Services Office) 
Tribal Groups 
AES has voluntarily contacted eight tribal groups to inform them about the proposed project. The Hopi 
Tribe expressed interest in further involvement and learning more about the project. AES will be working 
with the Hopi Tribe to continue the dialogue regarding the project.  
Media 
Legal notices will be presented to the following news outlet: The Tribune (serving central Navajo 
County). 
Adjacent Landowners 
Notification of adjacent landowners is described below: 
• Navajo County—Adjacent landowners within 1 mile of the project boundary will be notified by 
notice mailing. This includes approximately 105 parcels for notice.

<!-- page 904 -->

County Recommended Groups and General Public 
AES will also notify any interest groups as recommended by Navajo County. These groups will be added 
to the mailing list as requested. The County will also share contact information for persons that have 
expressed past interest in this area or type of project.

Dear Neighbor,  
AES is applying for a Special Use Permit from Navajo County and a Certificate of Environmental 
Compatibility from the Arizona Corporation Commission to construct and operate t he West Camp Wind 
Farm and associated gen -tie line, a maximum 500 -megawatt wind energy facility to be located almost 
entirely on private lands approximately 10 miles south west of Joseph City in unincorporated Navajo 
County, Arizona, as shown in the attached figure.  
The West Camp Wind Farm would be comprised of up to 104 wind turbines, and would include a parking 
area, storage facilities, an operations and maintenance building, access roads, permanent meteorological 
towers, and an Aircraft Detection Lighting System (ADLS) . The project’s generated electricity would 
connect to the power grid at the Arizona Public Service Cholla substation via an approximately 15 -mile-
long generation-tie line located north of the project area, which is planned to parallel existing high voltage 
infrastructure outside of the  wind farm project boundary. Energy generated by the wind facilities and 
energy stored in the battery storage facilities would be routed to up to two project substations via 34.5 -
kV underground collection lines. The wind turbine generators would have a total system height of up to 
820 feet. The project is sited in a remote location and incorporates a setback from the project boundary. 
Visual simulations, cultural resource investigations, natural resource and wildlife studies, and other siting 
evaluations are underway, in addition to ongoing agency consultation, to identify and mitigate impacts to 
applicable resources.   
Wind energy is building a cleaner future and creating economic benefits for all Arizonans.  The West Camp 
Wind Farm would bring many local and state benefits, including: 
• 500+ construction jobs and 20- 30 full-time local positions during the 25+ year operating life at 
full buildout 
• Property taxes and other local economic benefits for Navajo County 
• Lease payments to rural ranching families 
• The project is being designed to avoid impacts to sensitive environmental and cultural resources 
and sited to minimize impacts to residential areas   
• At full buildout, the project will generate electricity equivalent to powering over 300,000 homes 
annually, with no operational air emissions or water use  
• The property will remain a cattle ranch and the installation of wind facilities will not preclude or 
dramatically change existing land uses

West Camp Wind
Project details
 Æ System size: 500 MWac
 Æ Located in Navajo County, Arizona
 Æ Offsets the equivalent of 2 million tons of carbon 
dioxide per year
 Æ Approximately 500 jobs created during peak 
construction
 Æ Powers the equivalent of 368,935 homes annually
 Æ Estimated operation date: 2025
Bringing clean energy to every 
Arizonian
AES Community Impact Benefits
 Æ Contribute to Watts of Love, with the commitment 
to enhance access to safe, affordable electricity 
and lighting for off-the-grid communities
 Æ Support the Winslow Chamber of Commerce and 
Willow Bend Environmental Education Center
 Æ Support the Holbrook Chamber of Commerce
 Æ Partner with industry groups to provide solar 
workforce training programs to Arizona residents
 Æ Adhere to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s and 
Arizona Game and Fish Department’s wind energy 
wildlife guidelines to identify, avoid, minimize, and 
compensate for potential adverse impacts to 
wildlife resources thought to be at risk from wind 
energy development
 Æ Make lease payments to rural ranching families and 
landowners
 Æ Design the project thoughtfully and sustainably 
to avoid impacts to sensitive environmental and 
cultural resources and site it to minimize impacts to 
residential areas.
Find out more about our project at
www.aes.com/west-camp-wind
The 500 MW West Camp Wind facility will be located 
on mostly private lands about 10 miles south of Joseph 
City, Arizona. The wind farm will connect to Arizona’s 
power grid at the decommissioning Cholla Power Plant 
and supports the state’s renewable energy objectives. 
The proposed facilities for the project will include some 
of the most advanced wind energy technology deployed 
to date in Arizona. In addition to the wind turbines, the 
proposed on-site components for the project include an 
operations and maintenance building, up to two project 
substations, permanent meteorological towers, a 
switchyard, a high voltage project transmission line to 
connect to the grid, and access roads. The site will also 
feature a radar-activated lighting system that enables 
the federally required turbine lights to turn on only when 
low flying aircraft are in this remote area to preserve 
Northern Arizona’s dark sky characteristics. Energy 
storage may also be included as part of the project’s 
infrastructure. 
The West Camp facility is expected to generate 
approximately $15 million in tax revenue for the Navajo 
County area over the life of the project. At full project 
buildout, 500+ construction jobs will be needed and 
construction of the project generates increased 
economic activity in the surrounding communities.  
At peak production, West Camp Wind will generate 
enough energy to power approximately 368,935 homes 
and reduce CO2 emissions by the equivalent of about 2 
million tons, equivalent to 213,352,141 gallons of gasoline 
consumed.

TECHNICAL MEMORANDUM 
To: Rob Gardner 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC 
282 Century Place #2000 
Louisville, Colorado 80027 
From: Carlos Ituarte, Air Quality Specialist 
Date: June 22, 2022 
Re: West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment / SWCA Project No. 64382.01 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES Corporation (AES) is proposing 
to develop the West Camp Wind Farm (project), a maximum 500-megawatt alternating current nameplate 
capacity wind energy facility in Navajo County, Arizona. The project would be sited on private land and 
Arizona State Trust land administered by the Arizona State Land Department (ASLD) within 
an approximately 53,000-acre project area that is 10 miles southwest of Joseph City. The project 
is evaluating several generation-tie interconnection options to interconnect the project with the regional 
transmission grid, including one on-site interconnection option and two interconnection options at the 
Cholla Substation. The project is projected to achieve commercial operation in 2025, with construction 
beginning in late 2023 or early 2024.  
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10, Section 2008 requires that background (pre-development) 
sound levels be properly assessed, that sound levels be forecast in advance of Navajo County Special Use 
Permit (SUP) approval, and that, once a project commences operation, sound levels again be assessed 
as part of compliance-period assessment. Before an SUP is issued, the applicant’s independent consultant 
shall complete a sound evaluation by determining existing (pre-development) background sound levels 
and forecasting ambient sound levels anticipated upon completion of the facility. The evaluation shall 
address facility aging and planned or probable modifications. If the project is permitted and constructed, 
when it is in operation, the SUP holder’s independent consultant shall complete a compliance-period 
sound evaluation. 
SWCA Environmental Consultants (SWCA) prepared this technical memorandum to document the 
baseline noise conditions in the area and to estimate noise impacts that could result from the project. This 
assessment includes a SoundPLAN modeling exercise to model impacts to nearby noise sensitive areas 
(NSAs) based on the wind turbine layout and turbine specifications. 
The sound study was completed in accordance with the requirements of Section 2008 of the County 
zoning ordinance, as well as the Sound Requirement Guidelines for Wind Energy Generation Facilities 
as adopted by the County under Resolution 57-10. The placement of any turbines shall be in accordance 
with the results of the sound study and the noise requirement, mitigation measures, and physical setbacks, 
as identified in Section 2008 of the County Zoning Ordinance. The postconstruction sound study and 
monitoring shall be in accordance with Section 2008 of the County Zoning Ordinance.

<!-- page 945 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
2 
SWCA conducted a noise impact assessment using a project design that includes up to 104 turbines. The 
noise impact evaluation, provided herein, consists of computer noise modeling using SoundPLAN 
Essential Version 5.1 and assessment of the outputs as they pertain to the Navajo County sound (noise) 
standards and nearest NSA (i.e., nearest legal residence), which is approximately 1.3 miles (2.1 
kilometers) from the nearest proposed turbine.  
Estimated project sound levels were added to the assumed ambient levels to ascertain the degree 
of influence the ambient levels may have on determining compliance with County Zoning Ordinance 
No. 06-10, Section 2008 of the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance, and County Resolution No. 57-10. 
The noise impact assessment for the modified turbine locations and turbine type indicates the following: 
• The project would generate a daytime and nighttime noise level of up to 35.8 A-weighted decibels 
(dBA) at the closest legal residence (the NSA herein) from the nearest proposed turbine, resulting 
in an increase over ambient levels (33.6 dBA) that is 2.2 dBA. Thus, no significant increase at the 
closest NSA is expected from the operation of the project as the noise would not exceed the Navajo 
County Ordinance No. 06-10 of 45 dBA LAeq10. 
• Potential low-frequency noise (LFN) from the operation of the project does not exceed 68 decibels 
(dB) at 16 hertz (Hz), 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the closest NSA as required 
by Navajo County Resolution No. 57-10. 
• Under any ambient condition scenario, potential sound levels from the project would comply with 
all regulatory noise limits and guidelines established by County Zoning Ordinance No.  06-10 and 
County Resolution No. 57-10.  
Details regarding the project location, regulatory setting, existing ambient noise levels, and the approach 
and results of the noise impact assessments are included in the sections below.  
PROJECT LOCATION 
The appreciably 53,000-acre project site would be located on private and ASLD-administered land 
in Navajo County, approximately 10 miles south of Joseph City, Navajo County, Arizona. Land uses 
within the project site include cattle ranching/grazing and recreation (limited hunting). Arizona State 
Route 377 (Heber Road) runs north–south along the eastern edge of the project area. The closest NSA 
is a residence located approximately 1.3 miles northwest of the project’s nearest proposed turbine. 
ACOUSTICAL TERMS 
The following acoustical terms are used in this memorandum: 
• Ambient sound level is defined as the composite of noise from all sources near and far, 
the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location. 
• Decibel (dB) is the physical unit commonly used to measure sound levels. Technically, a dB 
is a unit of measurement that describes the amplitude of sound equal to 20 times the base 
10 logarithm of the ratio of the reference pressure to the sound of pressure, which 
is 20 micropascals. 
• Sound measurement is further refined by using a decibel “A-weighted” sound level (dBA) 
scale that more closely measures how a person perceives different frequencies of sound; the 
A-weighting reflects the sensitivity of the ear to low or moderate sound levels. The dBA scale 
is logarithmic; therefore, individual dBA values for different sources cannot simply be added

<!-- page 946 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
3 
together to calculate the sound level for the two sources. For example, two 50-dBA sources, 
added logarithmically, produce a collective noise level of 53 dBA. 
• Sound measurement can also be refined by using the “C-weighted” sound level (dBC) scale, 
typically used to specify peak or impact noise levels. Unlike the dBA scale, this weighed 
scale measures uniformly over lower frequencies and measures flat across the octave bands. 
The C-weighting may be used as an indicator of high levels of LFN.  
• Equivalent noise level (Leq) is the energy average A-weighted noise level during the 
measurement period. 
• Day-night sound level (Ldn) is the A-weighted equivalent sound level for a 24-hour period 
with an additional 10 dB weighting imposed on the equivalent sound levels occurring during 
night-time hours (10 p.m. to 7 a.m.).  
• Percentile sound level (Ln) is the A-weighted decibel value exceeded during n% of the 
measurement period. For example, L10 is a relatively loud noise exceeded only 10% of the 
measured time, whereas L90 is a relatively quiet sound exceeded 90% of the measured time. 
People tend to exhibit differing sensitivity to noise depending on the time of day, with noise 
generated at night being more noticeable than that generated during the day.  
SOUND LEVELS OF REPRESENTATIVE SOUNDS AND NOISES 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has developed an index to assess noise impacts from 
a variety of sources using residential receptors. If Ldn values exceed 65 dBA, residential development 
is not recommended (EPA 1974). Noise levels in a quiet rural area at night are typically between 32 and 
35 dBA. Quiet urban night-time noise levels range from 40 to 50 dBA. Noise levels during the day 
in a noisy urban area are frequently as high as 70 to 80 dBA. Noise levels above 110 dBA become 
intolerable; levels higher than 80 dBA over continuous periods can result in hearing loss. Levels above 
70 dBA tend to be associated with task interference. Levels between 50 and 55 dBA are associated with 
raised voices in a normal conversation. Constant noises tend to be less noticeable than irregular

REGULATORY SETTING 
Both federal and Navajo County laws are applicable to this project and the analysis of soundscape 
impacts. Applicable laws, regulations, and guidance include the following: 
• The EPA indicates that noise levels of 55 dBA Ldn or greater at residential land use would 
be considered a significant impact. 
• Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 and County Resolution No. 57-10. 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Public Health Threshold 
In 1974 the EPA published Information on Levels of Environmental Noise Requisite to Protect Public 
Health and Welfare with an Adequate Margin on Safety (EPA 1974). In this publication, the EPA 
evaluated the effects of environmental noise with respect to health and safety and determined an Ldn 
of 55 dBA (equivalent to a continuous noise level of 48.6 dBA) to be the maximum sound level that will 
not adversely affect public health and welfare by interfering with speech or other activities in outdoor 
areas. 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 
Section 2008 of County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 (Navajo County 2010a) contains wind 
energy–generating facility standards, which define a “Wind Energy Generating Facility” as an energy 
generation facility using wind technology and consisting of one or more wind turbines and accessory 
structures and buildings, including substations, anemometers, and associated electrical infrastructure, with 
an actual or planned generating capacity of at least 1 megawatt.  
According to Section 2008, noise levels due to project operations shall not exceed the greater of 45 dBA 
LAeq10 or the measured background (LA90,10 plus 5 dB) at the exterior of any legal residence, school, 
library, or hospital at the time of (build) permit approval. As allowed by Section 2008 (4)(v)(1)(B),

<!-- page 948 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
5 
a waiver showing the irrevocable written consent of the landowner can be issued in the event the 
operating noise levels exceed these limits.  
Navajo County Resolution No. 57-10 
Section 2008 also states that operational wind farms must meet requirements in County Resolution 
No. 57-10 Section 2 (Navajo County 2010b). Section 2 requires that background (pre-development) and 
compliance-period (post-development) sound levels shall be measured at locations that have received 
prior approval by Navajo County following applicable International Organization for Standardization 
(ISO), American National Standards Institute (ANSI), and Acoustical Society of America (ASA) 
standards that apply to noise measurements. 
Section 2 additionally requires that all wind farms meet the LFN and vibration requirements in ANSI 
S12.2 (RNC-25) and S12.9. Sound pressure levels for the 1/1 octave band shall not exceed 68 dB 
at 16 hertz (Hz), 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the exterior of any legal residence, school, 
library, or hospital at the time of (build) permit approval. 
Thresholds used to evaluate potential noise impacts are based on applicable criteria; noise from the 
project would be considered significant if the following occurs: 
• It exceeds 45 dBA LAeq,10 or the measured background (LA90,10) plus 5 dB at the exterior 
of any legal residence, school, library, or hospital, in accordance with Section 2008 of the 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance.  
• LFN levels exceed 68 dB at 16 Hz, 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the exterior 
of any legal residence, school, library, or hospital at the time of permit approval.

CALIBRATION CHECKS 
The sound level meter was calibrated at the beginning and end of each measurement period using a 
Larson Davis Model CAL200 Precision Acoustic Calibrator. The Larson Davis CAL200 emits a 1 kHz 
tone at 114 dB against which the response can be checked. The calibrator has been designed for both field 
and laboratory use, and the accuracy has been calibrated to a reference traceable to the National Institute 
of Standards and Technology.  
As recommended by Larson Davis, when using a free-field microphone, the pressure level at the 
microphone diaphragm will be slightly different. Thus, a free field correction of -0.12 dB was applied 
to the 114.0 dB tone. All four Larson Davis 831 SLMs demonstrated a calibration response with error 
levels below the typical 0.5 dB error allowed. The results for the calibrations are shown in Table 5.

NOISE IMPACT ASSESSMENT 
The following section provides results and interpretation of potential impacts from noise generated by the 
project during operation, as required by the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 (Navajo County 
2010a) and County Resolution No. 57-10 (Navajo County 2010b).  
This noise impact evaluation consists of computer noise modeling using SoundPLAN Essential Version 
5.1. Potential noise impacts were evaluated by determining the projected increases over ambient 
conditions using the loudest condition scenario model based on the maximum number of turbine locations 
and the noisiest of the proposed wind turbine options under consideration at that time. 
A total of 104 General Electric (GE) 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine generators (turbines) rated 
at 107.5 dBA were included in the analysis. Several turbine models are under consideration the project. 
For the purposes of this study, specifications from loudest of the turbine models were used to represent 
maximum sound levels. Other noise-producing project infrastructure (i.e., substations), located within the 
project site, were not included in this analysis because it was determined that the turbines would dominate 
the overall project’s acoustical output. 
A “Best estimate” sound power level octave band data from 13 Hz to 10 kHz were provided by the 
manufacturers as a function of wind speed at hub height. The GE 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine reaches its 
highest sound power level (107.5 dB) at wind speeds between of 10 m/s and 15 m/s. Table 8 lists the

Based on the sound power levels input for each turbine, or source (104 locations), SoundPLAN estimates 
noise contours of the overall project in accordance with a variety of standards, primarily ISO 9613-2:1996 
Acoustics standards for noise propagation calculations (ISO 1996).  
All sound propagation losses, such as geometric spreading, air absorption, ground absorption, and barrier 
shielding, are calculated in accordance with these recognized standards. The model accounts for reflection 
(i.e., from adjacent structures and the ground). The model uses industry-accepted propagation algorithms 
and accepts sound power levels (in decibels) provided by the manufacturer and other sources. For 
estimating noise levels at the closest NSA, the following three (3) meteorological conditions where 
assumed: 
1. Standard conditions, assuming a temperature of 10°C, a relative humidity of 70%, and an air 
pressure of 1013 mbar.

<!-- page 955 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
12 
2. Monsoon season, assuming a temperature of 23°C, a relative humidity of 33%, and an air pressure 
of 1013 mbar. Based on average conditions from June 15 - September 30 at the Winslow Municipal 
Airport.  
3. Annual average, assuming a temperature of 13°C, a relative humidity of 40%, and an air pressure 
of 1013 mbar. Based on the average annual conditions at the Winslow Municipal Airport. 
The ISO 9613-2 standard estimates sound pressure levels at a specified distance by subtracting the 
attenuation factors from the source sound power level for each source in octave frequency bands. 
Attenuation factors include geometrical divergence, atmospheric attenuation, ground effect, and barrier 
attenuation; these terms are defined as follows: 
• Geometrical divergence occurs as the source sound power is spread out over an increasing 
surface area (i.e., as the distance from the source increases). The estimated loss rate is the 
same for all frequencies. This is considered the most significant loss associated with 
propagation. Attenuation due to geometrical divergence is highly dependent on the distance 
between the source and the receiver. Direction also affects the noise level: (0°) direct line 
of sight noise level will be higher than (90°) direction line of sight to an emission point. 
Therefore, the differences in ground elevation, and receiver height and hub height (source 
height) are important parameters.  
• Losses due to atmospheric attenuation occur as the energy in the sound wave is transformed 
to heat.  
As this attenuation is frequency-dependent and high frequencies are more readily attenuated 
than low frequencies; these losses are highly influenced by humidity and temperature.  
• Ground effect is described according to the parameter Ground Factor (G) which varies 
between 0 for surfaces with low porosity (“hard” ground) and 1 for “soft” ground (surfaces 
including loose dirt, grass, crops, and other vegetation). This factor describes the effect 
of sound waves reflected off the ground. Parameters influencing the ground effect are the 
source height, receiver height, and propagation distance between the source and receiver and 
the ground conditions.  
• Barrier attenuation describes the effect of sound waves refracted around an imperforate 
element or barrier. A barrier could include man-made objects such as structures, buildings, 
and fences, as well as topographical features. Therefore, the differences in ground elevation, 
source height, receiver height, dimension, location absorption and reflection coefficients 
of man-made structures and topographic features are important parameters when estimating 
barrier attenuation in SoundPLAN. 
The following assumptions were made when running SoundPLAN: 
• Noise impact calculations were performed using octave band data from 13 Hz to 10 kHz.  
• Each wind turbine was modeled as individual point source at hub height. 
• Noise impacts at the NSA and depicted in the isopleths were estimated assuming a receiver 
height of 1.5 meters above ground level (AGL). 
• Elevations of the sources and of the receptors examined in the modeling were determined 
from United States Geological Survey Digital Elevation Map (DEM) and are based on North 
American Datum of 1927. Each of the DEM files had a 30-m resolution (7.5-minute DEM 
providing coverage of 7.5 × 7.5-minute blocks).

<!-- page 956 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
13 
• The proposed project was conservatively assumed to operate 24 hours per day, so the average 
noise output (including variations due to start-ups and shutdowns) would be essentially 
constant regardless of time of day.

Navajo County, Arizona 
April 29, 2022 
 
AES Clean Energy (AES) is proposing to develop a maximum 500-megawatt alternating current 
nameplate capacity wind energy facility in Navajo County, Arizona. The project would be sited on private 
lands within a 53,000-acre project area that is 10 miles southwest of Joseph City. The point of 
interconnection (Cholla substation) is 2 miles southeast of Joseph City (10 miles northeast of the 
proposed project area). The project is projected to achieve commercial operation in 2024. 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10, Section 2008 requires that background (pre-development) 
sound levels be properly assessed, that sound levels be forecast in advance of Navajo County Special 
Use Permit (SUP) approval, and that, once a project commences operation, sound levels again be 
assessed as part of compliance-period assessment. Before an SUP is issued, the applicant’s independent 
consultant shall complete a sound evaluation by determining existing (pre-development) background 
sound levels and forecasting ambient sound levels anticipated upon completion of the facility. The 
evaluation shall address facility aging and planned or probable modifications. If the project is permitted 
and constructed, when it is in operation the SUP holder’s independent consultant shall complete a 
compliance-period sound evaluation. 
The following details the proposed survey timeframe, noise level limits, monitoring locations, 
instrumentation, measurement procedures, data to be recorded, and report format to seek concurrence 
from the Navajo County Public Works Department prior to initiating the survey. 
Proposed Survey Timeframe 
We are tentatively targeting performing the pre-development noise survey the week of May 9th, but 
obviously this is weather and agency response dependent. 
Noise Level Limits 
In accordance with the Navajo County zoning ordinance , a project sound study will be performed in 
compliance with Section 2008. The County’s wind ordinance limits audible sound due to project 
operations to no greater than: a) 45 dBA LAeq,10; or b) the measured background, LA90,10 plus 5 dB, as 
measured at the exterior at any legal residence, school, library or hospital in existence at the time of 
approval of the SUP. All wind turbine operations shall meet the operational low-frequency sound 
requirements applicable to wind turbines as specified in the sound guidelines adopted, published, and 
amended from time to time by the Board of Supervisors.

residence within 1-mile of the Project.  
For the purposes of Planning and Zoning, a legal residence would be a residence that is permitted and 
has a Certificate of Occupancy. The location of the closest legal residence to the Project, was confirmed

An SWCA technician will deploy one (1) continuously recording integrating sound level meters meeting 
the Type 1 requirements of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) Specifications for Sound 
Level Meters (ANSI S1.4, 2014). Sound monitoring will be conducted in general accordance with the 
ASTM Standard Guide for Measurement of Outdoor A-Weighted Sound Levels (ASTM E1014-12, 2012). 
Details regarding the instrumentation and setup are summarized in Table 2.  
Table 2. Proposed Instrumentation 
Instrumentation Details  
Sound Level Meter 
Make: Larson Davis  Model: 831C 
The sound level meters (SLM) will be capable of measuring the full acoustic 
environment of the study area. The selected SLMs will be capable of 
measuring 28 to 140 dBA.  
Sound Level Calibrator 
Make: Larson Davis  Model: Model CAL200 
An acoustically coupled calibrator with adaptors necessary to fit the 
microphone will be used to assure the accuracy of the sound level meter 
and microphone. The acoustical calibrator shall have been thoroughly 
calibrated with equipment traceable to a recognized standards organization 
and following the recommendations of the instrument manufacturer. 
Windscreen 
A microphone windscreen will be used for all outdoor measurements. A 
windscreen of open cell foam will be placed over the microphone to protect 
it from moisture and wind effects. 
Bird Spike A bird spike was also used to deter birds from perching on the 
windscreen/microphone. 
Tripod 
A tripod at approximately 1.5 meters (5 feet) in height above the ground, 
approximated ear height of an adult human will be employed to ensure a 
steady and repeatable microphone position.

<!-- page 964 -->
Sound level meter measurements are subject to interference from differences in ambient conditions, 
such as wind, precipitation, and electromagnetic interference. The following ambient conditions will be 
observed during measurements and will determine whether testing is to occur. 
• Wind - Wind may influence sound level measurements, even with a windscreen in place. Data 
obtained during intervals when wind generated sound is influencing the measurements shall not 
be used. Wind speed data will not be measured at the monitoring sites during the measurement 
period. If wind data is required for data validation of modeling purposes, data from a nearby 
weather station will be used. The closest monitoring station is the Lx Ranch (KAZHOLBR5) 
located approximately 6 miles west southwest of Holbrook, Arizona. 
• Precipitation - Precipitation almost always influences outdoor sound levels. Rain or fallen snow 
may affect the propagation of sound so that sound levels may be different. Therefore, making 
measurements during precipitation or when pavement is wet, or snow covered is not 
recommended. The weather forecast will be checked prior to deploying the sound level meters 
and will be continuously monitored through the duration of the study. Data collected during 
precipitation events will be flagged and will be deemed unusable. 
• Power Lines - Electromagnetic radiation interference and acoustical interference in the form of 
audible noise can be created by power lines. Electromagnetic radiation may result in wild and 
unexpected swings of the sound level meter indicator. In high humidity conditions, noise from 
power lines can increase dramatically. Monitors will not be placed within 100 feet of any 
existing power lines; therefore, no acoustical interference is expected from electromagnetic 
radiation. 
Measurement Procedure 
The sound level meters will be prepared following the procedure presented in Table 3. 
Table 3. Noise Monitoring Equipment Preparation 
Instrument/Procedure Description Frequency 
Battery A battery check will be conducted on all 
instruments before field calibration and 
measurement. 
1-2 times daily. 
Calibration Sound level meters will be field calibrated at the 
beginning and end of each measurement period in 
accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. 
The calibrator used will be designed for both field 
and laboratory use, and the accuracy will be 
calibrated to a reference traceable to the National 
Institute of Standards and Technology. 
At the 
beginning 
and end of 
the 
measurement 
period.  
 
Microphone 
Orientation 
The microphone will be oriented in accordance 
with the manufacturer’s instructions and at a 
height between 1.2 to 1.5 meters (4 to 5 feet) 
above the ground. 
Once at the 
beginning of the 
measurement 
period.

<!-- page 965 -->
Instrument/Procedure Description Frequency 
Sound Meter Setup The sound level meters will be programmed to 
sample and store dBA, dBC, and unweighted one-
third octave band frequency data, 20-20,000 Hz 
sound level data including Lmin, Lmax, and median 
LAeq, LA10, LA50, and LA90, and community sound 
parameters. Response will be set to “fast.” Data 
will be recorded in 1-second and 1-hour intervals. 
Once at the 
beginning of the 
measurement 
period. 
 
Measuring and Data Recording 
Table 4 describes the data that is going to be recorded over the duration of the noise monitoring 
study. 
 
Table 4. Proposed Measuring and Data Recording 
Element Details  
Meteorological 
Conditions 
Measured wind speed, wind direction, relative humidity, and dry bulb 
temperature, and notes of the general sky condition will be obtained from 
the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) for 
each day of the survey on an hourly basis. SWCA proposes to rely on the Lx 
Ranch (KAZHOLBR5) located approximately 6 miles west southwest of 
Holbrook, Arizona, to document weather conditions during the survey. 
Measurement 
Locations 
Exact measurement locations will be plotted on a map with a brief 
description of the area, including ground cover. 
Dominant Noise 
Sources 
Characteristics of the dominant noise sources will be recorded as well as 
any acoustical events such as operation of machinery, aircraft, and sounds 
made by animals.

<!-- page 966 -->
Sound Levels 
Measured 
The SLMs will be programmed to sample and store dBA, dBC,  and 
unweighted one-third octave band frequency data, 20-20,000 Hz sound 
levels. The following parameters are to be recorded by the SLM and 
reported on an hourly basis: 
  
• Duration of the measurement;  
• Minimum sound level (Lmin);  
• Maximum sound level (Lmax);  
• Equivalent sound level (Leq);  
• Median noise level (LA50);  
• Residual noise level (LA90); and  
• Noise level that is exceeded 10% of the time (LA10).  
 
Start Time and Stop 
Time 
Start time, stop time, and date of the measurements and the serial number, 
type, and manufacturer of the sound level meter, microphone, and 
calibrator will be recorded for each monitoring location. 
Calibration 
Measurements 
Using the acoustical calibrator, the sound level meter indication before and 
after the measurement set will be recorded. Adjustments, if required, will 
be made at this time. If the change in the calibration reading is 1 dB or 
greater, the data gathered since the preceding calibration are considered 
invalid and will be discarded. 
Digital Audio 
Recordings 
Continuous audio digital recordings will be collected at all measurement 
locations. These recordings will be used to review any unusual sound 
sources and sound levels, and to determine common sound sources at the 
monitoring sites. At a minimum, recordings will be sampled at a rate of 16 
kilosamples per second (ksps) with compression. Audible sources will be 
identified and logged into a spreadsheet and presented in a table with the 
percent time that each source is audible by hour of day. Recording quality 
will be at a minimum 16-bit resolution. 
 
Sound Modeling and Impact Analysis 
To determine potential sound impacts on NSAs, a sound modeling effort will be performed. This 
scope includes preparation of a noise impact assessment report. The preliminary acoustical analysis 
will include review of the proposed project and its potential impacts on NSAs in proximity to the 
project by collecting manufacturer data for sound generating equipment and modeling those 
impacts on nearby NSAs. To accomplish the modeling, sound impacts will be determined using the 
SoundPLAN Essential Version 5.1 modeling platform. Model inputs will be based on a worst-case 
turbine alternative scenario (i.e., the loudest of the turbine models being considered). The model 
will be designed to assess the sound impacts from multiple sources and will take into consideration 
the effects of ground type, topography, vegetation, air, obstructions, and distance on the 
propagation of sound.  
Upon completion of the modeling exercise, a comparison will be made of the modeled sound levels 
at the site with allowable levels as defined in the County’s wind ordinance, and any exceedances will 
be identified. Short-term, long-term, and cumulative impacts, if any, resulting from the operation of 
the project will be identified.

<!-- page 967 -->
Based on the results of the pre-development sound monitoring and modeling, SWCA will provide a 
sound study report, which will include the following:  
• A brief project description of the project, including a summary of the physical parameters of 
the proposed project and assessment methodology;  
• A description of the existing conditions within the proposed project area;  
• Schematic map of the area; 
• Basic introduction to the noise fundamentals and descriptors of time averaged noise levels; 
• Brief description of the sound monitoring locations; 
• Description of the sound level meter used; 
• Description of the calibration sequences; 
• Discussion of the survey weather conditions; 
• Times, dates, and durations of measurements; and 
• Summary of the modeling results and potential impacts at the closest legal residence; and 
• Sound contour maps illustrating sound levels at a given distance, location of NSAs, and 
geographic features surrounding the project area.

In accordance with the County’s zoning ordinance, a project sound study
will be performed in compliance with Section 2008. The County’s wind
ordinance limits audible sound due to project operations to no greater
than: a) 45 dBA LAeq,10; or b) the measured background, LA90,10 plus 5
dB, as measured at the exterior at any legal residence, school, library or
hospital in existence at the time of approval of the SUP. All wind turbine
operations shall meet the operational low-frequency sound requirements
applicable to wind turbines as specified in the sound guidelines adopted,
published, and amended from time to time by the Board of Supervisors.

1 Introduction 
1.1 General 
This document summarizes the acoustic emission characteristics of 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine for all 
available modes of operation, including apparent sound power levels LWA,k, as well as uncertainty levels 
associated with the sound power levels and octave and 1/3rd-octave band apparent sound power levels. 
All provided sound power levels are A-weighted. 
GE continuously verifies specifications with measurements, including those performed by independent 
institutes. 
1.2 Wind Farm Noise Management (available as an option) 
In noise-constrained areas it is often necessary to adapt the wind turbine operation to satisfy far-field noise 
limits. GE offers a dedicated Farm Noise Management system that provides greater flexibility and higher energy 
yield than standard turbine controls. This advanced scheme allows to continuously adjust the farm operation 
based on the environmental variables that influence farm noise emission, essentially wind speed and wind 
direction. 
The Wind Farm Noise Management package includes the following service and hardware: 
 Park level noise propagation modeling and optimization of wind farm operation, 
 Table with optimum turbine set-points across the park as a function of wind speed and wind 
sector, and 
 Installation and commissioning of the Farm Noise Management Software Package.

power level.

Table 1: Overview of configurations for each apparent sound power level 
For each nominal sound power level, there is a corresponding nominal rotor speed and in some cases several 
nominal electrical power levels. For example, 106 dBA can be achieved at 9.7 rpm with nominal electrical power 
levels from 4800 kW to 5500 kW. Please note that the 117 m hub height is not compatible with operating 
modes 100 dBA to 106 dBA and 125.4 m hub height with modes 104 dBA to 106 dBA. 
The electrical power rating values may vary with actual turbulent conditions on site. More detailed information 
to the power performance can be found in the NRO power curve documents for this product. The 105 dBA to 
100 dBA NRO modes are intended and designed to achieve lower peak noise emission levels while optimizing 
turbine power performance. The main objective is to provide sound power levels aligned with the stricter noise 
emission requirements typically enforced during limited periods of time only. It is not expected that wind 
turbines would permanently operate in a given NRO setting, but rather would switch from Normal Operation to 
Noise Reduced Operation as needed for a fraction of the day. A continuous NRO activity would require a 
dedicated assessment from GE.

5 Uncertainty Levels 
The apparent sound power levels given above are mean values of representative batches of turbines under 
evaluation. Uncertainty levels are not included. The uncertainty levels uc, σP, σR and σT associated with 
measurements and mean values are described in IEC 61400-11 and IEC/TS 61400-14. 
For GE wind turbines, a typical value of σP = 0.8 dB can be assumed. 
The uncertainties for octave and 1/3rd-octave sound power levels are generally higher than for total sound 
power levels. Guidance is given in IEC 61400-11. 
6 IEC 61400-11 and IEC/TS 61400-14 Terminology 
 LWA,K is the wind turbine apparent sound power level (referenced to 10-12W) measured with A-
weighting as a function of wind speed. Derived from multiple measurement reports per IEC 61400-
11, it is considered to be a mean value. 
 uc is the measurement uncertainty for acoustic testing as defined in IEC 61400-11. It is not a 
characteristic of the product, but of the measurement, and cannot be specified by GE. For average 
testing conditions, typical values of uc are 0.7 dB – 1.0 dB. 
 σP is the 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 unit-to-unit product variation according to IEC/TS 61400-14. It is a 
characteristic of the product and can therefore be specified by GE (see chapter 5). 
 σR is the overall measurement testing reproducibility as defined in IEC/TS 61400-14. It is not a 
characteristic of the product, but of the measurements, and cannot be specified by GE. For typical 
testing according to IEC 61400-11, a value of σR = 0.5 dB is widely accepted. 
 σT is the total standard deviation combining both σP and σR (see IEC/TS 61400-14). 
7 Reference Documents 
 IEC 61400-11, wind turbine generator systems part 11: Acoustic noise measurement techniques, 
ed. 2.1 (2006-11), or ed. 3 (2012-11). 
 IEC/TS 61400-14, Wind turbines – part 14: Declaration of apparent sound power level and tonality 
values, ed. 1 (2005-03). 
 MNPT – Machine Noise Performance Test, Technical documentation.
