EXHIBIT E 
Noise Study

<!-- page 1343 -->
TECHNICAL MEMORANDUM 
To: Rob Gardner 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC 
282 Century Place #2000 
Louisville, Colorado 80027 
From: Carlos Ituarte, Air Quality Specialist 
Date: June 22, 2022 
Re: West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment / SWCA Project No. 64382.01 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES Corporation (AES) is proposing 
to develop the West Camp Wind Farm (project), a maximum 500-megawatt alternating current nameplate 
capacity wind energy facility in Navajo County, Arizona. The project would be sited on private land and 
Arizona State Trust land administered by the Arizona State Land Department (ASLD) within 
an approximately 53,000-acre project area that is 10 miles southwest of Joseph City. The project 
is evaluating several generation-tie interconnection options to interconnect the project with the regional 
transmission grid, including one on-site interconnection option and two interconnection options at the 
Cholla Substation. The project is projected to achieve commercial operation in 2025, with construction 
beginning in late 2023 or early 2024.  
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10, Section 2008 requires that background (pre-development) 
sound levels be properly assessed, that sound levels be forecast in advance of Navajo County Special Use 
Permit (SUP) approval, and that, once a project commences operation, sound levels again be assessed 
as part of compliance-period assessment. Before an SUP is issued, the applicant’s independent consultant 
shall complete a sound evaluation by determining existing (pre-development) background sound levels 
and forecasting ambient sound levels anticipated upon completion of the facility. The evaluation shall 
address facility aging and planned or probable modifications. If the project is permitted and constructed, 
when it is in operation, the SUP holder’s independent consultant shall complete a compliance-period 
sound evaluation. 
SWCA Environmental Consultants (SWCA) prepared this technical memorandum to document the 
baseline noise conditions in the area and to estimate noise impacts that could result from the project. This 
assessment includes a SoundPLAN modeling exercise to model impacts to nearby noise sensitive areas 
(NSAs) based on the wind turbine layout and turbine specifications. 
The sound study was completed in accordance with the requirements of Section 2008 of the County 
zoning ordinance, as well as the Sound Requirement Guidelines for Wind Energy Generation Facilities 
as adopted by the County under Resolution 57-10. The placement of any turbines shall be in accordance 
with the results of the sound study and the noise requirement, mitigation measures, and physical setbacks, 
as identified in Section 2008 of the County Zoning Ordinance. The postconstruction sound study and 
monitoring shall be in accordance with Section 2008 of the County Zoning Ordinance.

<!-- page 1344 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
2 
SWCA conducted a noise impact assessment using a project design that includes up to 104 turbines. The 
noise impact evaluation, provided herein, consists of computer noise modeling using SoundPLAN 
Essential Version 5.1 and assessment of the outputs as they pertain to the Navajo County sound (noise) 
standards and nearest NSA (i.e., nearest legal residence), which is approximately 1.3 miles (2.1 
kilometers) from the nearest proposed turbine.  
Estimated project sound levels were added to the assumed ambient levels to ascertain the degree 
of influence the ambient levels may have on determining compliance with County Zoning Ordinance 
No. 06-10, Section 2008 of the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance, and County Resolution No. 57-10. 
The noise impact assessment for the modified turbine locations and turbine type indicates the following: 
• The project would generate a daytime and nighttime noise level of up to 35.8 A-weighted decibels 
(dBA) at the closest legal residence (the NSA herein) from the nearest proposed turbine, resulting 
in an increase over ambient levels (33.6 dBA) that is 2.2 dBA. Thus, no significant increase at the 
closest NSA is expected from the operation of the project as the noise would not exceed the Navajo 
County Ordinance No. 06-10 of 45 dBA LAeq10. 
• Potential low-frequency noise (LFN) from the operation of the project does not exceed 68 decibels 
(dB) at 16 hertz (Hz), 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the closest NSA as required 
by Navajo County Resolution No. 57-10. 
• Under any ambient condition scenario, potential sound levels from the project would comply with 
all regulatory noise limits and guidelines established by County Zoning Ordinance No.  06-10 and 
County Resolution No. 57-10.  
Details regarding the project location, regulatory setting, existing ambient noise levels, and the approach 
and results of the noise impact assessments are included in the sections below.  
PROJECT LOCATION 
The appreciably 53,000-acre project site would be located on private and ASLD-administered land 
in Navajo County, approximately 10 miles south of Joseph City, Navajo County, Arizona. Land uses 
within the project site include cattle ranching/grazing and recreation (limited hunting). Arizona State 
Route 377 (Heber Road) runs north–south along the eastern edge of the project area. The closest NSA 
is a residence located approximately 1.3 miles northwest of the project’s nearest proposed turbine. 
ACOUSTICAL TERMS 
The following acoustical terms are used in this memorandum: 
• Ambient sound level is defined as the composite of noise from all sources near and far, 
the normal or existing level of environmental noise at a given location. 
• Decibel (dB) is the physical unit commonly used to measure sound levels. Technically, a dB 
is a unit of measurement that describes the amplitude of sound equal to 20 times the base 
10 logarithm of the ratio of the reference pressure to the sound of pressure, which 
is 20 micropascals. 
• Sound measurement is further refined by using a decibel “A-weighted” sound level (dBA) 
scale that more closely measures how a person perceives different frequencies of sound; the 
A-weighting reflects the sensitivity of the ear to low or moderate sound levels. The dBA scale 
is logarithmic; therefore, individual dBA values for different sources cannot simply be added

<!-- page 1345 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
3 
together to calculate the sound level for the two sources. For example, two 50-dBA sources, 
added logarithmically, produce a collective noise level of 53 dBA. 
• Sound measurement can also be refined by using the “C-weighted” sound level (dBC) scale, 
typically used to specify peak or impact noise levels. Unlike the dBA scale, this weighed 
scale measures uniformly over lower frequencies and measures flat across the octave bands. 
The C-weighting may be used as an indicator of high levels of LFN.  
• Equivalent noise level (Leq) is the energy average A-weighted noise level during the 
measurement period. 
• Day-night sound level (Ldn) is the A-weighted equivalent sound level for a 24-hour period 
with an additional 10 dB weighting imposed on the equivalent sound levels occurring during 
night-time hours (10 p.m. to 7 a.m.).  
• Percentile sound level (Ln) is the A-weighted decibel value exceeded during n% of the 
measurement period. For example, L10 is a relatively loud noise exceeded only 10% of the 
measured time, whereas L90 is a relatively quiet sound exceeded 90% of the measured time. 
People tend to exhibit differing sensitivity to noise depending on the time of day, with noise 
generated at night being more noticeable than that generated during the day.  
SOUND LEVELS OF REPRESENTATIVE SOUNDS AND NOISES 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has developed an index to assess noise impacts from 
a variety of sources using residential receptors. If Ldn values exceed 65 dBA, residential development 
is not recommended (EPA 1974). Noise levels in a quiet rural area at night are typically between 32 and 
35 dBA. Quiet urban night-time noise levels range from 40 to 50 dBA. Noise levels during the day 
in a noisy urban area are frequently as high as 70 to 80 dBA. Noise levels above 110 dBA become 
intolerable; levels higher than 80 dBA over continuous periods can result in hearing loss. Levels above 
70 dBA tend to be associated with task interference. Levels between 50 and 55 dBA are associated with 
raised voices in a normal conversation. Constant noises tend to be less noticeable than irregular 
or periodic noises. Table 1 presents sound levels for some common noise sources and the human response 
to those decibel levels.

REGULATORY SETTING 
Both federal and Navajo County laws are applicable to this project and the analysis of soundscape 
impacts. Applicable laws, regulations, and guidance include the following: 
• The EPA indicates that noise levels of 55 dBA Ldn or greater at residential land use would 
be considered a significant impact. 
• Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 and County Resolution No. 57-10. 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Public Health Threshold 
In 1974 the EPA published Information on Levels of Environmental Noise Requisite to Protect Public 
Health and Welfare with an Adequate Margin on Safety (EPA 1974). In this publication, the EPA 
evaluated the effects of environmental noise with respect to health and safety and determined an Ldn 
of 55 dBA (equivalent to a continuous noise level of 48.6 dBA) to be the maximum sound level that will 
not adversely affect public health and welfare by interfering with speech or other activities in outdoor 
areas. 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 
Section 2008 of County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 (Navajo County 2010a) contains wind 
energy–generating facility standards, which define a “Wind Energy Generating Facility” as an energy 
generation facility using wind technology and consisting of one or more wind turbines and accessory 
structures and buildings, including substations, anemometers, and associated electrical infrastructure, with 
an actual or planned generating capacity of at least 1 megawatt.  
According to Section 2008, noise levels due to project operations shall not exceed the greater of 45 dBA 
LAeq10 or the measured background (LA90,10 plus 5 dB) at the exterior of any legal residence, school, 
library, or hospital at the time of (build) permit approval. As allowed by Section 2008 (4)(v)(1)(B),

<!-- page 1347 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
5 
a waiver showing the irrevocable written consent of the landowner can be issued in the event the 
operating noise levels exceed these limits.  
Navajo County Resolution No. 57-10 
Section 2008 also states that operational wind farms must meet requirements in County Resolution 
No. 57-10 Section 2 (Navajo County 2010b). Section 2 requires that background (pre-development) and 
compliance-period (post-development) sound levels shall be measured at locations that have received 
prior approval by Navajo County following applicable International Organization for Standardization 
(ISO), American National Standards Institute (ANSI), and Acoustical Society of America (ASA) 
standards that apply to noise measurements. 
Section 2 additionally requires that all wind farms meet the LFN and vibration requirements in ANSI 
S12.2 (RNC-25) and S12.9. Sound pressure levels for the 1/1 octave band shall not exceed 68 dB 
at 16 hertz (Hz), 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the exterior of any legal residence, school, 
library, or hospital at the time of (build) permit approval. 
Thresholds used to evaluate potential noise impacts are based on applicable criteria; noise from the 
project would be considered significant if the following occurs: 
• It exceeds 45 dBA LAeq,10 or the measured background (LA90,10) plus 5 dB at the exterior 
of any legal residence, school, library, or hospital, in accordance with Section 2008 of the 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance.  
• LFN levels exceed 68 dB at 16 Hz, 65 dB at 31.5 Hz, and 63 dB at 63 Hz at the exterior 
of any legal residence, school, library, or hospital at the time of permit approval. 
AMBIENT NOISE SURVEY MEASUREMENT LOCATIONS 
The objective of the ambient noise survey is to establish pre-development noise levels at the closest legal 
residence within 1-mile of the project. For the purposes of Planning and Zoning, a legal residence would 
be a residence that is permitted and has a Certificate of Occupancy. The location of the closest legal 
residence to the project, was confirmed by the Navajo County Planning Department as the permitted 
structure located on APN 111-22-259 approximately 0.45 mile west of the project property boundary and 
1.3-miles northwest of the project’s nearest proposed turbine. 
SWCA prepared a pre-development study approach that was provided to the Navajo County Planning 
Department for review and approval. The approach was approved by Navajo County on May 2, 2022. 
A copy of the approach and email correspondence is included as Appendix A. 
SWCA collected a pre-development noise measurement at the nearest legal residence from the project 
property boundary on May 12th – 14th, 2022. The specific placement of the sound level meters was mainly 
determined by environmental and logistical constraints, and the location of the closest NSAs that was 
determined to be the nearest legal residence to the site. Specifically, the noise monitor was placed in the 
public right of way, on the north side of Siby Road, approximately 650 feet north of the identified nearest 
legal residence and approximately 0.45 miles west of the project property boundary. 
Due to the rural nature of the area and the absence of highway, airport, commercial and industrial noise 
sources, this location provided an ambient sound level that is representative of the area to the west of the 
project’s property boundary. In addition, using the nearest legal residence for the purposes of evaluating 
potential noise impacts provides an estimate of the highest impacts for the purposes of the noise impact

CALIBRATION CHECKS 
The sound level meter was calibrated at the beginning and end of each measurement period using a 
Larson Davis Model CAL200 Precision Acoustic Calibrator. The Larson Davis CAL200 emits a 1 kHz 
tone at 114 dB against which the response can be checked. The calibrator has been designed for both field 
and laboratory use, and the accuracy has been calibrated to a reference traceable to the National Institute 
of Standards and Technology.  
As recommended by Larson Davis, when using a free-field microphone, the pressure level at the 
microphone diaphragm will be slightly different. Thus, a free field correction of -0.12 dB was applied 
to the 114.0 dB tone. All four Larson Davis 831 SLMs demonstrated a calibration response with error 
levels below the typical 0.5 dB error allowed. The results for the calibrations are shown in Table 5.

READINGS 
Long-term monitoring was conducted from May 12 through May 14, 2022. The monitor placed at LT1 
began noise monitoring around 6 p.m. on May 12 and ended around midnight on May 14. Stoppages 
during measurements occurred to verify the collected data were valid and due to logistical constraints. 
An approximate total of 48 hours of noise measurement data were collected at LT1. Sound levels were 
recorded over each 1-minute and 1-hour interval. 
The sound level meters were programmed to sample and store A-weighted sound level data, including 
Leq, percentile levels and community sound parameters. The following gives a brief description of the 
methodology used for the sound data collection: 
• A-weighted sound level was selected. 
• Sound meter was set on “slow” response. 
• During noise measurements any dominant background noise source was noted. 
• Weather conditions were observed and documented. 
Field data sheets were completed during each visit and are provided in Appendix C of this report.

NOISE IMPACT ASSESSMENT 
The following section provides results and interpretation of potential impacts from noise generated by the 
project during operation, as required by the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10 (Navajo County 
2010a) and County Resolution No. 57-10 (Navajo County 2010b).  
This noise impact evaluation consists of computer noise modeling using SoundPLAN Essential Version 
5.1. Potential noise impacts were evaluated by determining the projected increases over ambient 
conditions using the loudest condition scenario model based on the maximum number of turbine locations 
and the noisiest of the proposed wind turbine options under consideration at that time. 
A total of 104 General Electric (GE) 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine generators (turbines) rated 
at 107.5 dBA were included in the analysis. Several turbine models are under consideration the project. 
For the purposes of this study, specifications from loudest of the turbine models were used to represent 
maximum sound levels. Other noise-producing project infrastructure (i.e., substations), located within the 
project site, were not included in this analysis because it was determined that the turbines would dominate 
the overall project’s acoustical output. 
A “Best estimate” sound power level octave band data from 13 Hz to 10 kHz were provided by the 
manufacturers as a function of wind speed at hub height. The GE 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine reaches its 
highest sound power level (107.5 dB) at wind speeds between of 10 m/s and 15 m/s. Table 8 lists the

Based on the sound power levels input for each turbine, or source (104 locations), SoundPLAN estimates 
noise contours of the overall project in accordance with a variety of standards, primarily ISO 9613-2:1996 
Acoustics standards for noise propagation calculations (ISO 1996).  
All sound propagation losses, such as geometric spreading, air absorption, ground absorption, and barrier 
shielding, are calculated in accordance with these recognized standards. The model accounts for reflection 
(i.e., from adjacent structures and the ground). The model uses industry-accepted propagation algorithms 
and accepts sound power levels (in decibels) provided by the manufacturer and other sources. For 
estimating noise levels at the closest NSA, the following three (3) meteorological conditions where 
assumed: 
1. Standard conditions, assuming a temperature of 10°C, a relative humidity of 70%, and an air 
pressure of 1013 mbar.

<!-- page 1354 -->
West Camp Wind Farm Noise Impact Assessment 
12 
2. Monsoon season, assuming a temperature of 23°C, a relative humidity of 33%, and an air pressure 
of 1013 mbar. Based on average conditions from June 15 - September 30 at the Winslow Municipal 
Airport.  
3. Annual average, assuming a temperature of 13°C, a relative humidity of 40%, and an air pressure 
of 1013 mbar. Based on the average annual conditions at the Winslow Municipal Airport. 
The ISO 9613-2 standard estimates sound pressure levels at a specified distance by subtracting the 
attenuation factors from the source sound power level for each source in octave frequency bands. 
Attenuation factors include geometrical divergence, atmospheric attenuation, ground effect, and barrier 
attenuation; these terms are defined as follows: 
• Geometrical divergence occurs as the source sound power is spread out over an increasing 
surface area (i.e., as the distance from the source increases). The estimated loss rate is the 
same for all frequencies. This is considered the most significant loss associated with 
propagation. Attenuation due to geometrical divergence is highly dependent on the distance 
between the source and the receiver. Direction also affects the noise level: (0°) direct line 
of sight noise level will be higher than (90°) direction line of sight to an emission point. 
Therefore, the differences in ground elevation, and receiver height and hub height (source 
height) are important parameters.  
• Losses due to atmospheric attenuation occur as the energy in the sound wave is transformed 
to heat.  
As this attenuation is frequency-dependent and high frequencies are more readily attenuated 
than low frequencies; these losses are highly influenced by humidity and temperature.  
• Ground effect is described according to the parameter Ground Factor (G) which varies 
between 0 for surfaces with low porosity (“hard” ground) and 1 for “soft” ground (surfaces 
including loose dirt, grass, crops, and other vegetation). This factor describes the effect 
of sound waves reflected off the ground. Parameters influencing the ground effect are the 
source height, receiver height, and propagation distance between the source and receiver and 
the ground conditions.  
• Barrier attenuation describes the effect of sound waves refracted around an imperforate 
element or barrier. A barrier could include man-made objects such as structures, buildings, 
and fences, as well as topographical features. Therefore, the differences in ground elevation, 
source height, receiver height, dimension, location absorption and reflection coefficients 
of man-made structures and topographic features are important parameters when estimating 
barrier attenuation in SoundPLAN. 
The following assumptions were made when running SoundPLAN: 
• Noise impact calculations were performed using octave band data from 13 Hz to 10 kHz.  
• Each wind turbine was modeled as individual point source at hub height. 
• Noise impacts at the NSA and depicted in the isopleths were estimated assuming a receiver 
height of 1.5 meters above ground level (AGL). 
• Elevations of the sources and of the receptors examined in the modeling were determined 
from United States Geological Survey Digital Elevation Map (DEM) and are based on North 
American Datum of 1927. Each of the DEM files had a 30-m resolution (7.5-minute DEM 
providing coverage of 7.5 × 7.5-minute blocks).

<!-- page 1355 -->

• The proposed project was conservatively assumed to operate 24 hours per day, so the average 
noise output (including variations due to start-ups and shutdowns) would be essentially 
constant regardless of time of day.

nameplate capacity wind energy facility in Navajo County, Arizona. The project would be sited on private 
lands within a 53,000-acre project area that is 10 miles southwest of Joseph City. The point of 
interconnection (Cholla substation) is 2 miles southeast of Joseph City (10 miles northeast of the 
proposed project area). The project is projected to achieve commercial operation in 2024. 
Navajo County Zoning Ordinance No. 06-10, Section 2008 requires that background (pre-development) 
sound levels be properly assessed, that sound levels be forecast in advance of Navajo County Special 
Use Permit (SUP) approval, and that, once a project commences operation, sound levels again be 
assessed as part of compliance-period assessment. Before an SUP is issued, the applicant’s independent 
consultant shall complete a sound evaluation by determining existing (pre-development) background 
sound levels and forecasting ambient sound levels anticipated upon completion of the facility. The 
evaluation shall address facility aging and planned or probable modifications. If the project is permitted 
and constructed, when it is in operation the SUP holder’s independent consultant shall complete a 
compliance-period sound evaluation. 
The following details the proposed survey timeframe, noise level limits, monitoring locations, 
instrumentation, measurement procedures, data to be recorded, and report format to seek concurrence 
from the Navajo County Public Works Department prior to initiating the survey. 
Proposed Survey Timeframe 
We are tentatively targeting performing the pre-development noise survey the week of May 9th, but 
obviously this is weather and agency response dependent. 
Noise Level Limits 
In accordance with the Navajo County zoning ordinance , a project sound study will be performed in 
compliance with Section 2008. The County’s wind ordinance limits audible sound due to project 
operations to no greater than: a) 45 dBA LAeq,10; or b) the measured background, LA90,10 plus 5 dB, as 
measured at the exterior at any legal residence, school, library or hospital in existence at the time of 
approval of the SUP. All wind turbine operations shall meet the operational low-frequency sound 
requirements applicable to wind turbines as specified in the sound guidelines adopted, published, and 
amended from time to time by the Board of Supervisors.  
Proposed Monitoring Locations 
The objective of the noise study is to establish pre-development noise levels at the closest legal 
residence within 1-mile of the Project.  
For the purposes of Planning and Zoning, a legal residence would be a residence that is permitted and 
has a Certificate of Occupancy. The location of the closest legal residence to the Project, was confirmed

<!-- page 1361 -->
by the Navajo County Planning Department as the permitted structure located on APN 111-22-259 
approximately 0.45 miles west of the Project property boundary. A copy of the email correspondence is 
provided as Attachment #1.  
SWCA proposes to take a pre-development noise measurement at the nearest legal residence from the 
project property boundary. Due to the rural nature of the area and the absence of highway, airport, 
commercial and industrial noise sources, this location would provide an ambient sound level that is 
representative of the area to the west of the project’s property boundary. In addition, using the nearest 
legal residence for the purposes of evaluating potential noise impacts will provide an estimate of the 
highest impacts for the purposes of the noise impact modeling.  SWCA proposes to deploy the noise 
monitor in the public right of way, on the north side of Siby Road, approximately 650 feet north of the 
identified nearest legal residence. A map showing the proposed monitoring location is provided as 
Figure 1 and described below in Table 1.

An SWCA technician will deploy one (1) continuously recording integrating sound level meters meeting 
the Type 1 requirements of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) Specifications for Sound 
Level Meters (ANSI S1.4, 2014). Sound monitoring will be conducted in general accordance with the 
ASTM Standard Guide for Measurement of Outdoor A-Weighted Sound Levels (ASTM E1014-12, 2012). 
Details regarding the instrumentation and setup are summarized in Table 2.  
Table 2. Proposed Instrumentation 
Instrumentation Details  
Sound Level Meter 
Make: Larson Davis  Model: 831C 
The sound level meters (SLM) will be capable of measuring the full acoustic 
environment of the study area. The selected SLMs will be capable of 
measuring 28 to 140 dBA.  
Sound Level Calibrator 
Make: Larson Davis  Model: Model CAL200 
An acoustically coupled calibrator with adaptors necessary to fit the 
microphone will be used to assure the accuracy of the sound level meter 
and microphone. The acoustical calibrator shall have been thoroughly 
calibrated with equipment traceable to a recognized standards organization 
and following the recommendations of the instrument manufacturer. 
Windscreen 
A microphone windscreen will be used for all outdoor measurements. A 
windscreen of open cell foam will be placed over the microphone to protect 
it from moisture and wind effects. 
Bird Spike A bird spike was also used to deter birds from perching on the 
windscreen/microphone. 
Tripod 
A tripod at approximately 1.5 meters (5 feet) in height above the ground, 
approximated ear height of an adult human will be employed to ensure a 
steady and repeatable microphone position.

<!-- page 1363 -->
Sound level meter measurements are subject to interference from differences in ambient conditions, 
such as wind, precipitation, and electromagnetic interference. The following ambient conditions will be 
observed during measurements and will determine whether testing is to occur. 
• Wind - Wind may influence sound level measurements, even with a windscreen in place. Data 
obtained during intervals when wind generated sound is influencing the measurements shall not 
be used. Wind speed data will not be measured at the monitoring sites during the measurement 
period. If wind data is required for data validation of modeling purposes, data from a nearby 
weather station will be used. The closest monitoring station is the Lx Ranch (KAZHOLBR5) 
located approximately 6 miles west southwest of Holbrook, Arizona. 
• Precipitation - Precipitation almost always influences outdoor sound levels. Rain or fallen snow 
may affect the propagation of sound so that sound levels may be different. Therefore, making 
measurements during precipitation or when pavement is wet, or snow covered is not 
recommended. The weather forecast will be checked prior to deploying the sound level meters 
and will be continuously monitored through the duration of the study. Data collected during 
precipitation events will be flagged and will be deemed unusable. 
• Power Lines - Electromagnetic radiation interference and acoustical interference in the form of 
audible noise can be created by power lines. Electromagnetic radiation may result in wild and 
unexpected swings of the sound level meter indicator. In high humidity conditions, noise from 
power lines can increase dramatically. Monitors will not be placed within 100 feet of any 
existing power lines; therefore, no acoustical interference is expected from electromagnetic 
radiation.

Measuring and Data Recording 
Table 4 describes the data that is going to be recorded over the duration of the noise monitoring 
study. 
 
Table 4. Proposed Measuring and Data Recording 
Element Details  
Meteorological 
Conditions 
Measured wind speed, wind direction, relative humidity, and dry bulb 
temperature, and notes of the general sky condition will be obtained from 
the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) for 
each day of the survey on an hourly basis. SWCA proposes to rely on the Lx 
Ranch (KAZHOLBR5) located approximately 6 miles west southwest of 
Holbrook, Arizona, to document weather conditions during the survey. 
Measurement 
Locations 
Exact measurement locations will be plotted on a map with a brief 
description of the area, including ground cover. 
Dominant Noise 
Sources 
Characteristics of the dominant noise sources will be recorded as well as 
any acoustical events such as operation of machinery, aircraft, and sounds 
made by animals.

<!-- page 1365 -->
Sound Levels 
Measured 
The SLMs will be programmed to sample and store dBA, dBC,  and 
unweighted one-third octave band frequency data, 20-20,000 Hz sound 
levels. The following parameters are to be recorded by the SLM and 
reported on an hourly basis: 
  
• Duration of the measurement;  
• Minimum sound level (Lmin);  
• Maximum sound level (Lmax);  
• Equivalent sound level (Leq);  
• Median noise level (LA50);  
• Residual noise level (LA90); and  
• Noise level that is exceeded 10% of the time (LA10).  
 
Start Time and Stop 
Time 
Start time, stop time, and date of the measurements and the serial number, 
type, and manufacturer of the sound level meter, microphone, and 
calibrator will be recorded for each monitoring location. 
Calibration 
Measurements 
Using the acoustical calibrator, the sound level meter indication before and 
after the measurement set will be recorded. Adjustments, if required, will 
be made at this time. If the change in the calibration reading is 1 dB or 
greater, the data gathered since the preceding calibration are considered 
invalid and will be discarded. 
Digital Audio 
Recordings 
Continuous audio digital recordings will be collected at all measurement 
locations. These recordings will be used to review any unusual sound 
sources and sound levels, and to determine common sound sources at the 
monitoring sites. At a minimum, recordings will be sampled at a rate of 16 
kilosamples per second (ksps) with compression. Audible sources will be 
identified and logged into a spreadsheet and presented in a table with the 
percent time that each source is audible by hour of day. Recording quality 
will be at a minimum 16-bit resolution. 
 
Sound Modeling and Impact Analysis 
To determine potential sound impacts on NSAs, a sound modeling effort will be performed. This 
scope includes preparation of a noise impact assessment report. The preliminary acoustical analysis 
will include review of the proposed project and its potential impacts on NSAs in proximity to the 
project by collecting manufacturer data for sound generating equipment and modeling those 
impacts on nearby NSAs. To accomplish the modeling, sound impacts will be determined using the 
SoundPLAN Essential Version 5.1 modeling platform. Model inputs will be based on a worst-case 
turbine alternative scenario (i.e., the loudest of the turbine models being considered). The model 
will be designed to assess the sound impacts from multiple sources and will take into consideration 
the effects of ground type, topography, vegetation, air, obstructions, and distance on the 
propagation of sound.  
Upon completion of the modeling exercise, a comparison will be made of the modeled sound levels 
at the site with allowable levels as defined in the County’s wind ordinance, and any exceedances will 
be identified. Short-term, long-term, and cumulative impacts, if any, resulting from the operation of 
the project will be identified.

<!-- page 1366 -->
Based on the results of the pre-development sound monitoring and modeling, SWCA will provide a 
sound study report, which will include the following:  
• A brief project description of the project, including a summary of the physical parameters of 
the proposed project and assessment methodology;  
• A description of the existing conditions within the proposed project area;  
• Schematic map of the area; 
• Basic introduction to the noise fundamentals and descriptors of time averaged noise levels; 
• Brief description of the sound monitoring locations; 
• Description of the sound level meter used; 
• Description of the calibration sequences; 
• Discussion of the survey weather conditions; 
• Times, dates, and durations of measurements; and 
• Summary of the modeling results and potential impacts at the closest legal residence; and 
• Sound contour maps illustrating sound levels at a given distance, location of NSAs, and 
geographic features surrounding the project area.

1 Introduction 
1.1 General 
This document summarizes the acoustic emission characteristics of 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 wind turbine for all 
available modes of operation, including apparent sound power levels LWA,k, as well as uncertainty levels 
associated with the sound power levels and octave and 1/3rd-octave band apparent sound power levels. 
All provided sound power levels are A-weighted. 
GE continuously verifies specifications with measurements, including those performed by independent 
institutes. 
1.2 Wind Farm Noise Management (available as an option) 
In noise-constrained areas it is often necessary to adapt the wind turbine operation to satisfy far-field noise 
limits. GE offers a dedicated Farm Noise Management system that provides greater flexibility and higher energy 
yield than standard turbine controls. This advanced scheme allows to continuously adjust the farm operation 
based on the environmental variables that influence farm noise emission, essentially wind speed and wind 
direction. 
The Wind Farm Noise Management package includes the following service and hardware: 
 Park level noise propagation modeling and optimization of wind farm operation, 
 Table with optimum turbine set-points across the park as a function of wind speed and wind 
sector, and 
 Installation and commissioning of the Farm Noise Management Software Package.

2 Overview of Configurations 
The following table presents an overview of the configurations associated with each nominal apparent sound 
power level.

Table 1: Overview of configurations for each apparent sound power level 
For each nominal sound power level, there is a corresponding nominal rotor speed and in some cases several 
nominal electrical power levels. For example, 106 dBA can be achieved at 9.7 rpm with nominal electrical power 
levels from 4800 kW to 5500 kW. Please note that the 117 m hub height is not compatible with operating 
modes 100 dBA to 106 dBA and 125.4 m hub height with modes 104 dBA to 106 dBA. 
The electrical power rating values may vary with actual turbulent conditions on site. More detailed information 
to the power performance can be found in the NRO power curve documents for this product. The 105 dBA to 
100 dBA NRO modes are intended and designed to achieve lower peak noise emission levels while optimizing 
turbine power performance. The main objective is to provide sound power levels aligned with the stricter noise 
emission requirements typically enforced during limited periods of time only. It is not expected that wind 
turbines would permanently operate in a given NRO setting, but rather would switch from Normal Operation to 
Noise Reduced Operation as needed for a fraction of the day. A continuous NRO activity would require a 
dedicated assessment from GE.

4 Octave Band Spectra and 1/3rd Octave Band Spectra

modes at different hub height wind speeds. The corresponding wind speeds at 10 m height for all available 
towers are provided in Annex I. Operational information, including rated electrical power and rotor speed are 
listed along with each set of spectra.  Additionally, the list of compatible towers for each mode is also provided.

5 Uncertainty Levels 
The apparent sound power levels given above are mean values of representative batches of turbines under 
evaluation. Uncertainty levels are not included. The uncertainty levels uc, σP, σR and σT associated with 
measurements and mean values are described in IEC 61400-11 and IEC/TS 61400-14. 
For GE wind turbines, a typical value of σP = 0.8 dB can be assumed. 
The uncertainties for octave and 1/3rd-octave sound power levels are generally higher than for total sound 
power levels. Guidance is given in IEC 61400-11. 
6 IEC 61400-11 and IEC/TS 61400-14 Terminology 
 LWA,K is the wind turbine apparent sound power level (referenced to 10-12W) measured with A-
weighting as a function of wind speed. Derived from multiple measurement reports per IEC 61400-
11, it is considered to be a mean value. 
 uc is the measurement uncertainty for acoustic testing as defined in IEC 61400-11. It is not a 
characteristic of the product, but of the measurement, and cannot be specified by GE. For average 
testing conditions, typical values of uc are 0.7 dB – 1.0 dB. 
 σP is the 4.x/5.x/6.x-158 unit-to-unit product variation according to IEC/TS 61400-14. It is a 
characteristic of the product and can therefore be specified by GE (see chapter 5). 
 σR is the overall measurement testing reproducibility as defined in IEC/TS 61400-14. It is not a 
characteristic of the product, but of the measurements, and cannot be specified by GE. For typical 
testing according to IEC 61400-11, a value of σR = 0.5 dB is widely accepted. 
 σT is the total standard deviation combining both σP and σR (see IEC/TS 61400-14). 
7 Reference Documents 
 IEC 61400-11, wind turbine generator systems part 11: Acoustic noise measurement techniques, 
ed. 2.1 (2006-11), or ed. 3 (2012-11). 
 IEC/TS 61400-14, Wind turbines – part 14: Declaration of apparent sound power level and tonality 
values, ed. 1 (2005-03). 
 MNPT – Machine Noise Performance Test, Technical documentation.

Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
1 
1 INTRODUCTION 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES Corporation (AES), is proposing to 
develop a maximum 500-megawatt wind energy facility and associated generation-tie transmission line in 
Navajo County, Arizona. This Visual Impact Assessment presents the anticipated visual impact of the 
proposed West Camp Wind Farm (Project) to the surrounding area. The Project area consists of the wind 
farm boundary and generation-tie transmission line route options (Figure 1). Included in the assessment 
are (1) a description of the characteristic landscape in the Project vicinity and (2) an evaluation of 
potential visual impacts based on photo-realistic simulations from Key Observation Points (KOPs) and a 
visual contrast analysis. All work presented here was performed by SWCA Environmental Consultants 
(SWCA). 
2 METHODS 
The SWCA visual resource specialist conducted a field visit to the Project area and vicinity in April 2022 
to (1) gain an understanding of the general landscape character that would potentially be affected by 
construction and operation of the proposed Project, (2) identify KOPs for Project review and data 
collection, and (3) take photographs from each KOP to support the creation of photo-realistic visual 
simulations. 
2.1 KOP Identification 
KOPs are vantage points from where the proposed Project may be visible from publicly accessible 
locations. The KOPs were identified in coordination with the Applicant and Navajo County planning staff 
and represent views of persons in residential areas and in vehicles traveling along residential or regional 
roadways where the proposed Project would be seen (Figure 1). 
2.2 Photography and Visual Simulations 
Photo simulations, which provide a theoretical view or depiction of the Project, were prepared for each 
KOP. A digital rendering of the Project components was superimposed on the KOP baseline photographs 
to illustrate a simulated representation of how the Project may appear based on conditions observed 
during the documentation of the baseline photography using a 50mm equivalent focal length. The photo 
simulations were used as a tool to aid in evaluating the level of potential visual contrast and associated 
impacts of the Project before and after construction. Due to the constraints of replicating on-the-ground 
conditions, how an observer may perceive the Project in a three-dimensional environment based on visual 
acuity (ability to recognize small details with precision), as well as perceiving Project movement (real 
world) as compared to a two dimensional static photo simulation, the photo simulations may not represent 
all conditions or situations in which the Project may be viewed or perceived by viewers (e.g., variability 
in atmospheric, seasonal, and lighting conditions could influence the view). The duration of the view may 
vary as well; for example, a viewer driving Arizona State Highway 377 versus a viewer standing at Obed 
Road. The impact analysis is not solely based on photo simulations and only demonstrates a potential 
viewing condition while taking into consideration how the Project may be perceived within the landscape 
over time and under variable conditions.

<!-- page 1417 -->
Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
2 
 
Figure 1. Key Observation Point (KOP) locations for the West Camp Wind Farm Visual Simulations 
and Contrast Analysis.

<!-- page 1418 -->
Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
3 
Photo-realistic simulated views of the Project were developed using ArcGIS, Google Earth Pro, Autodesk 
products (AutoCAD and 3ds Max), and Adobe Photoshop for each KOP. Using these programs, the 
proposed layout of the wind turbines was modeled, then the images (or “models”) of the layout were 
superimposed onto the panoramic photographs taken during the field visits. The simulations were 
developed by superimposing a three-dimensional computer model of the proposed Project components on 
a digital elevation model and then placing that onto the base photographs at the correct scale and distance. 
Date and time-of-day inputs determine shadows and reflected light, and the software accounts for distance 
and haze to increase accuracy of viewing conditions at the time the base imagery was taken. Following 
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) guidelines for turbine marking standards, the RAL Color 
Standard (RAL Number 7035 [Light Grey]) has been replicated in the photo simulation process, which, 
as noted by the FAA, is the color used for most wind turbines currently produced (FAA 2020). 
The specifications of the modeled turbine, the Siemens Gamesa 6.0 MW, are: (1) hub height of 540 feet, 
(2) rotor diameter of 560 feet, and (3) total height of 820 feet. The specification of the modeled 345 kV 
monopole transmission line are: (1) total height of 180 feet. 
2.3 Contrast Analysis 
A visual contrast analysis is a qualitative discussion of anticipated contrast between the existing landscape 
and the proposed activities and facilities. Factors taken into consideration for such an analysis include 
distance of the proposed project elements from the viewer and the level of perceived contrast between the 
proposed project elements and the existing landscape. These factors are further defined below. 
The distance zones for evaluating impacts to scenery are: 
• Foreground: up to 1 mile 
• Middle Ground: 1 to 3 miles 
• Background: 3 miles and beyond 
The level of perceived contrast between the proposed project elements and the existing landscape is 
classified using the following definitions:  
• None: The element contrast is not visible or perceived.  
• Weak: The element contrast can be seen but does not attract attention.  
• Moderate: The element contrast begins to attract attention and begins to dominate the 
characteristic landscape.  
• Strong: The element contrast demands attention, would not be overlooked, and is dominant in the 
landscape. 
2.4 Shadow Flicker 
A wind turbine’s moving blades can cast a moving shadow on locations within a certain distance of a 
turbine. These moving shadows are called shadow flicker. The extent of shadow flicker depends on the 
time of year and day (which determine the sun’s azimuth and altitude angles) and the wind turbine’s 
physical characteristics (height, rotor diameter, blade width, and orientation of the rotor blades). Shadow 
flicker does not occur when the sun is obscured by clouds or fog, at night, or when the source turbines are 
not operating. Shadow flicker intensity is defined as the difference in brightness at a given location in the 
presence and absence of a shadow and the intensity diminishes with greater receptor-to-turbine separation 
distance. Shadow flicker intensity for receptor-to-turbine distances beyond approximately 1.25 miles is

<!-- page 1419 -->
Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
4 
very low and generally considered imperceptible. In general, shadow flicker becomes more noticeable as 
one gets closer to turbines, with the largest number of shadow flicker hours, along with greatest shadow 
flicker intensity, occurring nearest the wind turbines. 
The shadow flicker assessment was conducted using the EMD International windPRO Shadow Module 
software, that models the occurrence of shadow flicker for the proposed turbine scenario (location and 
turbine type). The software presents the total amount of time (hours and minutes per year) and location 
where shadow flicker would occur in the turbine vicinity and at relevant sensitive receptor locations.  
3 RESULTS 
3.1 Characteristic Landscape 
The landscape in the vicinity of the proposed Project is characterized by flat open areas with minor 
undulations in topography. Vegetation consists mainly of large areas of light-colored (sage and light 
green) perennial grasses, forbs, and shrubs interspersed with dense, extensive sagebrush flats. Pinyon 
juniper forest occur within the Project area and dot the landscape with irregularity. The Project area lies 
southwest of Joseph City, Arizona occurring on a sprawling mesa top. There are minor drainages and 
minor canyon country within the area. 
The most notable scenic features in the landscape are the Hopi Buttes located north of Joseph City. These 
dark, jagged, volcanic buttes rise to a maximum of 6,480 feet above sea level and are prominent features 
in the broad, slightly undulating landscape. These features host low indistinct grasses and have a sporadic 
distribution of pinyon juniper woodlands. Light, vibrant, exposed soils contrast with dark grey basalt. 
Petrified Forest National Park resides approximately 22 miles to the northeast of the Project area and is 
bisected by Interstate 40.  
The landscape within the Project area is mostly undeveloped but has been partially modified by human-
made structures and activities. Roads, ranch infrastructure, and transmission lines have contributed to 
changes to the natural landscape within the Project area, as have scattered rural residences located on 
subdivided lands west of the Project area. Numerous improved and unimproved dirt roads occur within 
the vicinity as well as Arizona State Highway 377, Arizona State Highway 99, and Interstate 40, a 
primary transportation thoroughfare for southwest states. Additional human modification to the landscape 
includes range improvements such as the occasional earthen and metal stock tanks, corrals, and ranch 
outbuildings. With the exception of existing high voltage transmission line infrastructure, the overall 
character of the landscape can be considered rural rangeland. 
3.2 Visual Simulations and Contrast Analysis by KOP 
SWCA in coordination with the Applicant (AES) and Navajo County, Arizona planning staff, identified 
and photo documented five KOPs. The locations of these KOPs are shown in Figure 1, and the visual 
simulations to support each KOP are included in Appendix A. 
Impacts to visual resources were determined by examining the simulated condition and evaluating the 
degree of change in landscape character (i.e., degree to which Project elements contrast with existing 
conditions) that would result from the construction and operation of the proposed West camp Wind 
Project. The visual impact analysis for each of the five KOPs is provided below.

<!-- page 1420 -->
Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
5 
3.2.1 KOP 1: Interstate 40 and Frontage Road 
KOP 1 represents the potential views of vehicles traveling on Interstate 40. The photographs were 
collected along an adjacent frontage road approximately 9.1 miles northeast of the nearest wind turbine 
(see Figure 1). Views in the immediate foreground consist of a smooth, consistent, distinctive roadway 
with contrasting paint markings along with small, stippled, patches of sage green vegetation with 
contrasting red-brown to khaki-colored exposed soils. This offramp and corresponding terrain gently 
slope towards the Project area. Larger amorphic trees appear along the banks of the Little Colorado River 
and colors range from grey to bright green. Views in the midground consist of a continuous, smooth beige 
to brown coloration with stippled, isolated dark greens of pinyon juniper woodlands. The landform 
throughout the area consists of soft undulations and relative flat topography. Tall, subtle, repetitive, light 
gray geometric lattice transmission structures are backdropped against the beige to brown vegetation. 
Views in the background consist of dark green pinyon juniper that is dense and carpet-like as it transitions 
to the horizon. The pinyon juniper woodland is minimal compared to the sprawling desert grasslands. 
From this KOP, the viewer is approximately 9.1 miles northeast of the nearest wind turbine. Based on the 
viewer’s superior perspective, distance to Project components and the backdrop of a consistently level 
topography, light sky color, Project components would not dominate the visual setting, but would be 
perceivable to the casual viewer. However, the wind turbines would introduce new forms, lines, colors, 
and textures not common within the landscape but would remain visually subordinate due to other 
infrastructure projects within the area. The overall distance from the KOP and the expansive views begin 
to absorb the Project visually. Project components would create weak contrast. 
3.2.2 KOP 2: Obed Road 
This KOP represents the view of a vehicle traveling north along Obed Road, approximately 0.9 mile south 
of the proposed generation-tie (gen-tie) corridor for gen-tie options interconnecting the Project at the 
Cholla Substation (see Figure 1). Views in the immediate foreground consist of a smooth, consistent, 
distinctive roadway with contrasting paint markings along with indistinct, low grasses and exposed soils. 
Vegetation colors range from light tans to sage greens while exposed soils consist of red-browns. Terrain 
remains level and flat. Throughout the foreground and middle ground, there are dark repeating barbed-
wire fences, overhead electric lines, tall weathered grey lattice transmission structures and a 
communication tower that add vertical elements to the landscape. Landform views in the middle ground 
consist of distinct, undulating, and continuous brown to light grey vegetation with small uplifts in the 
distance. Views in the background consists of soft uplifted buttes with darker exposed soils. 
From this KOP, the viewer would be approximately 0.9 mile south from the intersection of Obed Road 
and the gen-tie. Based on the viewer’s neutral perspective and alike transmission infrastructure within the 
area, the gen-tie would be perceived but would not dominate the view. Project components would create 
weak contrast and absorb into the existing landscape. 
3.2.3 KOP 3: Lx Ranch Road and Angel Light Lane 
KOP 3 represents general residential views from the residential area northeast of the proposed Project. 
Photographs were collected at the intersection of Lx Ranch Road and Angel Light Lane, approximately 
6.5 miles northeast of the nearest wind turbine (see Figure 1). Views in the immediate foreground are 
represented by green, grey, beige, and light tan vegetation contrasting with an existing dirt road. 
Geometric fence lines, gates, transmission line structures, and street signs give the landscape a disjointed 
characteristic compared to the natural landscape. The landform is flat and continuous with a slight uplift 
toward the Project area. Middle ground to background views are shielded by this uplift.

<!-- page 1421 -->
Visual Resource Assessment for the West Camp Wind Farm 
 
6 
From this KOP, the viewer is approximately 6.5 miles northwest of the nearest wind turbine. Based on the 
neutral viewing perspective, and distance to the nearest wind turbine along with the backdrop of the pale 
sky and existing vertical elements, the wind turbines would be perceivable within the landscape with 
turbine blade movement potentially attracting attention of the casual observer. Project components would 
introduce elements/patterns that would be visually evident but overall would have weak to moderate 
contrast, compared with other human made features in the landscape.  
3.2.4 KOP 4: Arizona State Route 377 
This KOP represents the view of a vehicle traveling along State Route 377, approximately 3.2 miles east 
of the nearest wind turbine (see Figure 1). Views in the immediate foreground consist of a stippled, 
consistent, short stature, desert grassland with regularly spaced small patches of exposed soils. Vegetation 
colors vary from tans to bright greens. Exposed soils are brown. Short, dark, repeating barbed wire fence 
posts are also within the foreground. Views in the middle ground consist of flowing, continuous lines 
with dark green pinyon juniper with smooth to coarse transitions of soft tan grasses between the 
undulating rolling hills.  
From this KOP, the viewer is approximately 3.2 miles east of the nearest wind turbine. Based on the 
viewer’s inferior perspective, and the backdrop of pale blue sky, the light-colored turbine structures, 
Project components would dominate the visual setting, and attract attention of the casual observer. 
The wind turbines would introduce new forms, lines, colors, and textures not common within the 
landscape. Project components would introduce vertical elements/patterns and movement from spinning 
turbine blades that would be visually prominent and create moderate to strong contrast, compared with 
other features in the landscape during short durations of views based on travel speeds. 
3.2.5 KOP 5: Hutch Road 
This KOP represents the view of a vehicle traveling along Hutch Road, approximately 2.5 miles west of 
the nearest wind turbine (see Figure 1). It also represents potential views from residential properties in the 
vicinity of Hutch Road. Views in the immediate foreground consist of smooth, khaki-colored, distinctive 
with short stature, continuous, tan grasses. Views in the middle ground consist of distinct pockets and 
broken dark green to light green pinyon juniper with smooth to coarse transitions of soft tan grasses 
between the flowing, subtle hills. Views in the background consist of uniform browns with pockets of 
dark green pinyon juniper. 
From this KOP, the viewer is approximately 2.5 miles west of the nearest wind turbine. Based on the 
viewer’s inferior perspective, and the backdrop of pale blue sky with no topographical constraints, the 
turbine structures, Project components would dominate the visual setting and attract attention of the 
casual observer. The wind turbines would introduce new forms, lines, colors, and textures not common 
within the landscape and movement from spinning turbine blades. Project components would introduce 
elements/patterns that would be visually prominent and create strong contrasts, compared with other 
features in the landscape. 
3.3 Shadow Flicker 
The shadow flicker model for the West Camp Wind Farm is presented in Figure 2. As illustrated, there 
would be no shadow flicker impact at the nearest legal residence as identified by Navajo County.

To address potential effects to other wildlife species, wildlife habitat, human safety, and
wildlife-oriented recreation, the Department recommends the following measures:
● Development of an adaptive weed and erosion mitigation plan, covering construction and
operational phases of the project, that addresses road shoulders and disturbed areas,
including provisions for preventing the spread of invasive species and re-seeding with
native species.
● If milkweed plants are present, please avoid removal to the extent possible. These plants
are important for monarch butterflies, which are a candidate for listing under the
Endangered Species Act and are declining throughout their range.
● Artificial lighting can attract nocturnal animals (including birds and bats), impair their
ability to navigate, and may affect their behaviors (Davies et. al. 2013). Federal Aviation6
Administration (FAA)-required red lighting should be installed on turbines according to
FAA guidelines for wind energy (FAA 2020). If additional lighting is needed near the7
ground, consider using only the minimum amount necessary for safety. Motion-sensing
lights and narrow-spectrum lighting are preferred, as well as ensuring that all lighting is
fully shielded and dark-sky compliant (USFWS 2012 ).8
● To reduce impacts on hunters, the Department requests continued coordination on
proposed starting/ending times for construction so the Department can adjust tag numbers
if necessary and/or notify constituents of closures during proposed hunts and seasons.
Notification of the construction timeline will also enable the Department to account for
any adjustments to access agreements with the lessee.
Finally, Department staff routinely conduct low level wildlife survey and monitoring flights. The
Department requests that AES provide coordinates for any new meteorological evaluation towers
(METs) installed or decommissioned during the project. These coordinates will be incorporated
into a database and shared with Department pilots to protect the safety of personnel conducting
low-altitude flights.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on the West Camp Wind Farm. The Department
looks forward to continued collaboration as this project progresses. For further coordination,
please contact Tiffany Sprague at tsprague@azgfd.gov or 623-236-7222.

Environmental Studies

<!-- page 1451 -->
Exhibit H-1 
EXHIBIT H. ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES 
A Noise Study and a Visual Resource Assessment were completed for the Project and are included in this 
application as Exhibit E and Exhibit F, respectively. Additional completed, ongoing, or planned 
environmental studies are discussed below. 
Wildlife Site Characterization 
A Wildlife Site Characterization was completed for the Project to gather existing information about the 
wildlife community potentially using the site and to identify additional data collection or information 
needs. That report is appended to this exhibit as Attachment A. 
Wildlife Survey Plan 
A Wildlife Survey Plan was prepared for the Project and reviewed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 
and Arizona Game and Fish Department. The plan, which is appended to this exhibit as Attachment B, 
describes the methods for site-specific preconstruction wildlife surveys that were initiated at the site on 
behalf of a different developer and are ongoing or will be resumed in the future. Studies addressed in the 
report include the following: 
• Eagle and Other Large Bird Use Surveys 
• Small Bird Use Surveys 
• Eagle Nest Surveys 
• Non-eagle Species Nest Surveys 
• Bat Acoustic Surveys 
Preliminary Jurisdictional Delineation for Waters of the U.S. 
A desktop review of wetlands and other waters of the U.S. was completed in June 2022. The evaluation 
memorandum summarizing the results of the initial desktop review and outlining future steps to be taken 
in the delineation process is appended to this exhibit as Attachment C. The results of the desktop research 
indicated that there are ephemeral surface water features present that may be potentially jurisdictional 
waters of the U.S. These include ephemeral drainages (washes) and stock tanks (ponds). Additionally, the 
Little Colorado River is located just south of the Cholla Substation and is intersected by the Gen-Tie Line 
Corridor to the Cholla Substation exterior to the Wind Farm Site. To the extent practicable, the Project 
will be designed to avoid surface water features. Project components including the turbines, substations, 
switchyard, operations and maintenance facility, and laydowns yards will avoid placement in surface 
waters. Transmission line structures will also span surface waters. Some temporary and permanent 
crossings of ephemeral drainages (washes) may be required for access roads and collection lines. Because 
the affected drainages at crossings are likely to be protected under the Clean Water Act (i.e., 
“jurisdictional”) and thus subject to permitting requirements under Section 404 of that Act, the Applicant 
will conduct a preliminary delineation of waters of the U.S. and obtain necessary permits as required prior 
to construction.

<!-- page 1452 -->
Exhibit H-2 
Cultural Resource Surveys  
A desktop review of AZSITE, Arizona’s online cultural resources database, was conducted to identify 
previous cultural resources investigations and known cultural resources in and within proximity of the 
Wind Farm Site and the Gen-Tie Line Corridor to the Cholla Substation. In addition to the AZSITE 
database, the National Park Service’s National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) online database was 
also searched to identify properties listed in the NRHP. The St. Joesph Bridge, an NRHP-listed property, 
is located approximately 1 mile west of the Cholla Substation. Constructed in 1917, the bridge spans the 
Little Colorado River at Obed Road. It is recognized for being one of the larger county-built structures in 
Arizona and one of the few multiple-span vehicular trusses remaining in the state. The AZSITE database 
shows that four surveys have partially overlapped with the Gen-Tie Line Corridor to the Cholla 
Substation. One site (AZ P:3:1[ASM]) is depicted as partially overlapping with the Gen-Tie Line 
Corridor to the Cholla Substationand five additional sites are located 0.08 mile to 0.1 mile (132–317 
meters) away. AZ P:3:1(ASM), also known as the Hashknife Range, is a historic-era site consisting of a 
portion of the Aztec Land and Cattle Company’s cattle range ranched in the 1880s and 1890s. No 
additional information is provided and the site was not evaluated for its eligibility for listing in the 
National or Arizona Registers of Historic Places (N/ARHP). Because of sparse cultural resources 
investigations, the AZSITE data may not adequately represent the potential density of cultural resources 
that may be present in the Wind Farm Site and the Gen-Tie Line Corridor to the Cholla Substation. In 
addition to the previous investigations mentioned above, 27 additional cultural resources surveys have 
been conducted within a 3-mile radius. For cultural resources, 101 site numbers have been assigned 
within the 3-mile radius. Site types include Native American artifact scatters, Puebloan habitation sites 
ranging from small temporary, limited activity sites to walled structures, and petroglyph sites. There 
are also documented resources associated with historic-era activities in the area, including artifact 
scatters, habitations, and in-use structures. Twelve sites have been recommended or determined eligible, 
three sites have been recommended as ineligible, and 92 have not been evaluated for listing in the 
N/ARHP. 
The Applicant will retain qualified archaeologists to conduct pedestrian surveys of all areas on State Land 
potentially disturbed by construction of the planned Wind Farm. Such surveys are required on State Trust 
land by the State Historic Preservation Act of 1982 (Arizona Revised Statutes [ARS] 41-861–864) and 
the Arizona Antiquities Act of 1960, amended in 1981 (ARS 41-841–844) and their implementing 
regulations. Although not required by any law or regulation, the Applicant will also conduct cultural 
resources surveys on private land in coordination with the landowner.  
Because construction of the planned Wind Farm has no federal nexus, federal laws regarding effects on 
cultural resources do not apply. Arizona state laws and regulations regarding effects on cultural resources 
on State Trust land, however, do apply. According to the ASLD, the appropriate treatment of a potentially 
affected cultural resource on State Trust land depends upon its eligibility for listing in the Arizona 
Register of Historic Places (ARHP). If a site on State Trust land is determined to be ineligible for listing 
in the ARHP, no further work is required. If a site on State Trust land is determined to be eligible for 
listing in the ARHP, it should be avoided. If avoidance is not possible, or desirable, then mitigation for 
adverse effects is required.   
In constructing the planned Wind Farm, the Applicant intends to avoid any sites recommended as 
register-eligible located on both private and State Trust land. If avoidance of a register-eligible site is 
impracticable, the Applicant will abide by all applicable laws and regulations regarding treatment of the 
site.

<!-- page 1453 -->
Exhibit H-3 
Native Plant Inventory 
All Arizona Protected Native Plants on State Trust land that may be removed or destroyed during project 
construction will be counted and the state compensated for the loss of those plants. To identify qualifying 
plants, biologists will conduct native plant surveys on State Trust land within the requested right-of-way 
areas in accordance with the ASLD Native Plant Survey Protocol. Per that protocol, random sample plots 
will be established based on Natural Resources Conservation Service soil data, and all protected plants in 
the plots counted. Plant counts from the sample plots for each unique vegetation type/soil type 
combination will be totaled and extrapolated in the final Native Plant Inventory reporting based on the 
number of acres in each unique combination for the portion of the Project on State Trust land. The 
extrapolated plant totals from each unique vegetation/soil combination will then be tallied for an overall 
total by species. As required by the protocol, the surveyors will also note the presence of any non-native 
invasive plant species.  
Phase I Environmental Site Assessment 
A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment will be completed for the project in late 2022 or 2023.

Wildlife Site Characterization for the West Camp Wind Farm 
i 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES Corporation (AES), is proposing to 
develop a wind energy facility in Navajo County, Arizona. The proposed 52,500-acre project area is 
located on private and state lands approximately 10 miles south of Joseph City. The project is evaluating 
several generation-tie (gen-tie) options, including one interconnection option within the project area 
(wind development area) and two interconnect options with a gen-tie corridor external to the project area. 
For the purposes of this report, the project area and external gen-tie corridor are distinguished from each 
other. SWCA Environmental Consultants prepared this wildlife site characterization to provide an initial 
landscape-scale screening and site-level characterization of the proposed project. The report addresses the 
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Land-Based Wind Energy Guidelines Tiers 1 and 2 (preliminary site 
evaluation and site characterization) and Eagle Conservation Plan Guidance Stage 1 (site assessment), as 
well as the Arizona Game and Fish Department’s (AGFD’s) Guidelines for Reducing Impacts to Wildlife 
from Wind Energy Development in Arizona.  
Objectives were addressed through desktop evaluation of publicly available information, communication 
with AGFD’s experts, a site visit on January 27, 2022, and repeated visits to the site (on foot and by 
helicopter) during initial preconstruction wildlife surveys from October 2019 to November 2021. A 
summary of findings and next steps is presented in the last section of this report. The purpose of this 
evaluation is to: 
• Address federal and state guidance landscape-scale screening and site-level characterization 
objectives, including gathering an understanding of the wildlife community potentially using the 
site. 
• Determine additional data collection or information needs at this stage. Specific data gaps 
identified in this report include the following: 
o The extent to which special-status species are present. 
o The extent to which important golden eagle use areas (e.g., occupied eagle nests, or 
concentrated flight paths indicating areas that the species would rely on for breeding, feeding, 
or sheltering activities) are present within or near the project footprint. 
o Location and characterization of other areas of seasonal importance (e.g., bat maternity 
colonies or hibernacula sites, raptor nests). 
o Specific baseline bird and bat species composition and use (temporal and spatial). 
o Compensation requirements associated with Arizona Native Plant Law–protected species in 
areas of State lands planned for development. 
o Whether there would be significant adverse impacts to special-status species, considering the 
design of the project. 
Upon delivery of this report, AES is requesting a recommendation letter for the project from AGFD’s 
Project Evaluation Program to support county and line siting permitting. 
Tier 3 preconstruction wildlife surveys and reporting, which will provide quantitative and qualitative 
assessments used to further evaluate risk and make siting and operational decisions, are ongoing.

1 INTRODUCTION 
West Camp Wind Farm, LLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of The AES Corporation (AES), is proposing 
to develop the West Camp Wind Farm (project). The project is a proposed maximum 500-megawatt 
(MW) wind energy facility and associated generation-tie (gen-tie) transmission line. The project would 
be located almost entirely on private lands, with minor utilization of Arizona State Trust lands, within 
an approximately 52,500-acre project area 10 miles southwest of Joseph City, Navajo County, Arizona 
(Figures 1 and 2). A federal nexus is not anticipated for the siting of this project.  
The project is evaluating several gen-tie options to interconnect with the regional transmission grid. These 
options include up to 11-mile-long gen-tie and onsite line-tap within the project area (wind development 
area), or a 17-mile or 25-mile-long gen-tie connecting the project to the Arizona Public Service (APS) 
Cholla Substation 2 miles southeast of Joseph City. The gen-tie options with an interconnection to the 
Cholla Substation include a 150-foot-wide corridor external to the project area (Figure 1 and 2). Within 
the project area, the gen-tie options would be sited within 500-foot-wide corridors; however, the specific 
location of the internal corridors are not yet known. In this report, the term project area is inclusive of the 
internal gen-tie corridors and the term gen-tie refers only to the external gen-tie corridor. Further 
definitions for project terminology used in this report are provided in Section 2.2 below.  
The purpose of this report is to provide an initial landscape-scale screening and site-level characterization 
of the proposed project to address the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (USFWS’s) Land-Based Wind 
Energy Guidelines (WEG; USFWS 2012) Tiers 1 and 2 (preliminary site evaluation and site 
characterization) and Eagle Conservation Plan Guidance (ECPG) (USFWS 2013) Stage 1 (site 
assessment), as well as the Arizona Game and Fish Department’s (AGFD’s) Guidelines for Reducing 
Impacts to Wildlife from Wind Energy Development in Arizona (AGFD 2012a) preliminary site screening 
objectives. This report answers the following questions, to the extent they can be answered at this stage, 
which are meant to 1) identify potential impacts to wildlife, and 2) categorize eagle risk at this stage: 
• Are special-status species or their habitats (including designated critical habitat) present or likely 
to be present? 
• Are plant communities of concern present or likely to be present? 
• Are there high-priority conservation areas for non-governmental organizations, or other local, 
state, regional, federal, tribal, or international designations? 
• Are there large areas of intact habitat with the potential for fragmentation, with respect to species 
of concern needing large contiguous blocks of habitat? 
• Are their known critical areas of wildlife congregation or other areas of seasonal importance? 
• Are there important eagle use areas or migration concentration sites present? 
• How is the site categorized with respect to USFWS’s ECPG site categorization criteria? 
This report is being submitted after an initial wildlife agency coordination meeting, which was held 
on May 18, 2022. A Navajo County Special Use Permit (SUP) and an Arizona Corporation Commission 
(ACC) Certificate of Environmental Compatibility (CEC) will be pursued in the third and fourth quarters 
of 2022, with an SUP application anticipated to be delivered to Navajo County on June 23, 2022. Tier 3 
(preconstruction wildlife surveys) are underway, initiated by a different developer from October 2019 
through March 2020 and continued by AES from May 2020 through November 2021. These surveys will 
continue in 2023.
